en: *Lebang Wenlei*, Volume One, with Preface, Compiled by the Śramaṇa Zongxiao of Shizhi in Siming. Preface to *Lebang Wenlei*:
During the Qiandao era, His Majesty the Emperor personally inscribed the two characters "Lotus Society" (*Lianshe*) with his imperial brush at the Deyou Palace and bestowed them [upon the community].
The Regional Commander and General Governor of the Western Route of Zhejiang, Zhang Xi,
possesses all eight methods of calligraphy— dragon-soaring and phoenix-fluttering—
in their entirety. He is truly a rare auspicious omen of the Yellow and Luo Rivers.
I humbly reflect that Emperor Gaozong,
through the transformative influence of the ages of Tang and Yu, molded and refined the world; yet,
having achieved such merit, he did not dwell upon it.
Having cast aside the station of ten thousand chariots,
in the leisure of his reclusion,
he allowed his mind to roam within the inner scriptures.
Furthermore, desiring to restore the tradition of nianfo (Buddha-recitation) on Mount Lu,
he undertook this endeavor.
He examined throughout history how successive emperors had caused the Śākya teachings to flourish.
Some were those who established stupas and temples;
some were those who translated sutras and treatises;
and some were those who extensively ordained monks and nuns.
Yet I have never heard of anyone who, wielding brush and pen,
has expounded upon the Pure Land so as to enable all people to ascend and emerge from the five turbidities,
such as our Sage Ruler.
To this day, from within and beyond the vast seas, people revere the ancients and establish societies;
the sound of reciting the Buddha’s name resounds everywhere, filling the ears.
Thus we know that supreme virtue is like the wind.
The people should be like grass;
there are things that happen spontaneously without being expected.
Allow me to discuss this further.
Our Buddha, the Able One (Śākyamuni), was born in Kapilavastu;
yet, without lingering for the precious rank of the Golden Wheel-turning King,
he went directly to the Snowy Mountains to sit in meditative repose.
Having already attained the Way,
he expounded the teachings according to the capacities of beings;
thus, there came to be distinctions among the various doctrines of the Great and Small Vehicles, the Partial and the Perfect.
Finally, at the sublime assembly of the Lotus Sūtra, the single path is without partiality;
it opens the provisional vehicles so that all may return to the ultimate reality.
This was the original intention for his appearance in the world.
It is only now that [the Dharma] has begun to flourish.
Furthermore, I reflect upon the people of future generations,
whose faculties will be dull and obscured, such that they will be unable to seek liberation for themselves.
It is solely because Amitābha’s original vow takes one to the Land of Ultimate Bliss that one may cross the river of craving horizontally and directly transcend to the stage of Buddhahood.
Regarding the various Mahāyāna sūtras,
there have been many earnest exhortations to approach them;
this is surely the Tathāgata’s extraordinary and wondrous skillful means.
To examine and console those who have sunk into obscurity is what is meant by the saying that when a father departs, he leaves behind medicine.
However, as the Great Teaching has flowed eastward, some people may not yet understand it.
Now, during the Eastern Jin dynasty, Dharma Master Huiyuan possessed a spirit and intellect of extraordinary brilliance;
he was the first to open the source of transformation.
He diverted water to plant lotuses and established a Pure Society (*śuklavatī-saṃgha*).
At that time, there were one hundred and twenty-three participants.
With Liu Yimin and seventeen others as the preeminent leaders among the eighteen great worthies,
the practice of the Buddha-remembrance samādhi (nianfo sanmei) flourished from that time on.
To this day, more than eight hundred years have passed.
The lingering influence and enduring legacy remain imposingly present; thus,
it was possible for Zhang Yue to carry out the restoration.
One must follow in their footsteps from afar.
Thus, in pursuing learning one must seek a teacher;
in advancing in one's practice one must rely upon the Dharma.
Therefore, in the establishment of this society,
we shall take Amitābha alone as our presiding lord and the various sutras as our guiding compass.
Since the Jin and Tang dynasties,
eminent monks and great scholars have all composed writings to praise this matter.
Although within these works there are variations in the depth of their meaning and the skillfulness of their phrasing—
just as ten thousand streams flow eastward to converge in the vast blue sea—
they ensure that all who partake of them shall be moistened by the same single flavor.
Zongxiao, as he approached the twilight of his years,
realized that the world is not solid or enduring,
and he looked up with reverence to Emperor Gaozong.
His Way encompasses Heaven and Earth;
his virtue surpasses that of Fuxi and Xuanyuan.
Yet he still proclaimed and spread the ultimate teaching.
If one is to enlighten the ignorant masses,
how much more so for a fool like myself who has the misfortune of being ranked among the clergy—
how could I dare to be negligent regarding the path of reflection and cultivation?
Thereupon, he encompassed all the sutras and gathered together various compositions;
he prostrated himself before them and read them.
My intention has been to provide a sound guidance;
although its subtle phrasing and profound meaning are not easily fathomed,
I have studied and savored it for many years.
I have roughly grasped its general outline.
I reflect further that the Sui-jade and He-bi pearls are the most precious treasures in the world.
If one were to wrap it in a case and store it away,
who would then be able to share it with others?
Thus, on a day of leisure...
I have arranged them in sequence according to what I have obtained,
beginning with scriptures and incantations and concluding with poetry and prose,
comprising fourteen categories in total.
In total, there are more than two hundred and twenty verses,
divided into five fascicles,
titled *Lebang Wenlei* (Categorized Writings on the Land of Bliss).
This is modeled after the Confucian scholar Liu Zongchuan’s *Xihan Wenlei* (Classified Anthology of Western Han Prose).
Should there be works not included herein,
those who share my aspirations shall continue this collection in due time.
In total, there are forty-six locations throughout the various sutras where the Great Canon specifically discusses the Pure Land. The catalog of these sutras and treatises includes:
the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* (on the beginning of the Buddha’s transformative activities within the traces of Amitābha);
the *Karunāpuṇḍarīka-sūtra* (on the causal vows and the bestowal of predictions regarding the names of the Three Sages); and the *Bodhisattvotpatti-sūtra* (on the birth of the Bodhisattvas).
The Sutra on the Immeasurable Life Explaining the Causes and Practices of Amitābha for Accomplishing Sentient Beings;
The Dharma-Storehouse Sutra on the Vows for Adorning the Wondrous Land; The Sutra of Verses on Amitābha;
The Sutra on the Characteristics of Amitābha’s Original Vows for Attaining His Land; The Śūraṅgama Samādhi Sūtra.
The Great Power Attainer’s Attainment of the Perfect Penetration of Mindfulness of the Buddha;
the Drum-Sound King Sūtra on the City and Parents and Relatives in Amitābha’s Land;
the Amitābha Sūtra stating that the Land of Ultimate Bliss is beyond hundreds of thousands of billions of buddha-fields; the Amitābha Sūtra.
Not being distracted for seven days, one is moved by the Buddha to attain rebirth.

According to the *Sukhāvatīvyūha-sūtra*, by practicing the three types of karma, one attains birth in the Western Land. Regarding the initial cultivation of the visualization of the sun (*sūrya-vipaśyanā*) in the *Sukhāvatīvyūha-sūtra*: one sends forth one's thoughts toward the Western Land. *Sukhāvatīvyūha-sūtra* (Contemplation Sutra). The Visualization of the Sun. Sending the Mind to the West. *Sukhāvatīvyūha-sūtra*.

The eighth is the Contemplation of the Image (*xiàngguān*). Regarding contemplating the Buddha through the mind, the *Sukhāvatīvyūha-sūtra* states that one attains rebirth by means of three kinds of minds.
Regarding the achievement of the merit of ten recitations for the lowest of the low grade of rebirth, the *Amitāyurdhyāna-sūtra* [provides the details].
The attendants of Vaidehī all attained rebirth; the *Amitābha Sūtra* [states this occurs] through a mind of doubt;
the *Sukhāvatīvyūha Sūtra* [states it occurs] by being born within the womb of Amitāyus at the edge of the Western Realm;
and the *Bodhisattvagatyutpatti Sūtra* [describes] the Bodhisattva’s dwelling and birth within the womb.
*The Sutra of Equal Enlightenment* on falling into the Land of Sloth and Pride due to giving rise to a mind of defiled attachment;
*The Sutra of Immeasurable Life* on the śrāvakas practicing and realizing the fruit in the Pure Land;
*The Sutra of Immeasurable Life* on the exclusion of those who commit the five heinous crimes or slander the Dharma from attaining rebirth there.
The characteristics of rebirth through the cultivation of causes by the three grades;
the comparison in the *Sukhāvatīvyūha Sūtra* of the differences in the cultivation of goodness in the two lands;
the vast number of bodhisattvas reborn in the Pure Land according to the *Sukhāvatīvyūha Sūtra*; the *Sukhāvatīvyūha Sūtra*.
The Sutra on the Extinction of the Dharma Remaining for One Hundred Years; The Sutra on the Infinite Life Span of the Deliverance of Immeasurable People;
The Sutra on Encouraging All to Exert Diligence and Strive to Seek [the Way];
The Sutra on the Universal Radiance of the Buddha of Infinite Life; The Sutra on the Buddha of Infinite Life.
The precious bowl naturally overflows with food and drink;

the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* compares the length of day and night in two lands; Mañjuśrī’s exposition of the *Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* on the single practice samādhi consisting solely in the invocation of the Buddha's name; and the *Pratyutpanna Samādhi Sūtra*.
Cultivating the Samādhi of Establishing the Buddha and single-mindedly recollecting Amitābha according to the Vaipulya Mahāsaṃnipāta Sūtra;
within the method of contemplating the Middle Way of the Samādhi of Establishing the Buddha,
the Elder Vimukta attained the gate of mindfulness of the Buddha as being solely mind, according to the Avataṃsaka Sūtra.
By relying on the vows of Samantabhadra, one attains rebirth in Sukhāvatī;
by hearing and practicing the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, one immediately attains rebirth there;

according to the *Mahāratnakūṭa-sūtra*, by generating ten kinds of mind, one attains rebirth in Sukhāvatī; and according to the *Sukhāvatīvyūha-sūtra*, one attains rebirth in accordance with one's vows.
In this Sahā world of turbidity and evil, there are the *Mahāsannipāta-ratnaketu-dhāraṇī-sūtra* which extols the West;
the *Buddhānusmṛti-samādhi-sūtra* where one sees the Buddha according to one's mind, whether large or small; the *Maudgalyāyana-paripṛcchā-sūtra*;
and the *Sukhāvatīvyūha-sūtra* (Ten Recitations Sutra) concerning the Land of Immeasurable Life, which is easy to access and easy to attain.
The *Buddhānusmṛti-sūtra* (Sutra on the Protection of Those Who Practice Buddha-Recollection); the *Buddhanusmṛti-samādhi-sūtra* (Sutra on the Samadhi of Contemplating the Buddha);
the *Mañjuśrī-buddhakṣetraguṇavyūha-sūtra* (Sutra on the Prediction that Mañjuśrī Shall Be Born in Sukhāvatī);
the *Mañjuśrī-praṇidhāna-sūtra* (Sutra on Mañjuśrī’s Vow); and the *Laṅkāvatāra-sūtra*.
The *Buddha’s Record of Nāgārjuna’s Rebirth in the Land of Bliss*, the *Sūtra on Good Faith and Mākyin*,
the *Sūtra on Good Faith’s Disgust for Womanhood and Aspiration for Rebirth in the Western Land*,
the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* which discusses the high or low status of retribution based on the quantity of emotional attachments and perceptions, and the *Sūtra of the Sovereign Who Protects the Realm*.

The Ritual for the Contemplative Practice and Offerings to Amitāyus, which contains ten dhāraṇīs for the superior or inferior retribution experienced after death according to one’s good or evil deeds, extracts three dhāraṇīs as follows: the Mantra of the Fist-Mudrā of Tathāgata Amitāyus; the Root Mudrā Mantra of Tathāgata Amitāyus; and the Heart Mantra of Tathāgata Amitāyus. From the *Uṣṇīṣa-vijaya-dhāraṇī-sūtra*, one dhāraṇī is extracted as follows: the Dhāraṇī Method of Tathāgata Amitāyus. From the *Amoghapāśa-kalparāja-mantra-sūtra*, three dhāraṇīs are extracted as follows: the Ekākṣara-mantra (Single-Syllable Mantra); and the Sarvatraga-vimukti-citta-mantra (Mantra of the Mind of Universal Liberation).

The Amoghapāśa-mahābhiṣeka-prabhā-mantra; the Biography of Amitābha’s Inconceivable Supernatural Power; the Treatise on Attaining Birth by Eradicating the Root of All Karmic Obstructions; the General Overview in Six Sections; the Sūtra of Immeasurable Life; the Verses on Rebirth;
the Exegesis on the Fivefold Method of Practice; the Commentary on the Easy Path of Mindfulness of the Buddha; and the Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra.
For those who delight in accumulating merit and seek rebirth in a Pure Land,

the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* distinguishes between the pure and impure lands of Śākyamuni and Amitābha; the *Mahāyāna-śraddhotpāda-śāstra* emphasizes that in this Sahā world one does not encounter a Buddha,
and thus exclusively encourages mindfulness and contemplation as the essential method.

Catalogue of Sūtras and Śāstras Exclusively Concerning the Pure Land from the Great Canon, for those of both sharp and dull faculties who contemplate the Buddha’s marks and signs and the honorific title of Amitābha Buddha. I have compiled and categorized these texts.
The reason for first presenting the sutras and śāstras is that those who wish to cultivate pure karma must attend to their fundamental basis;
these various sutras and śāstras are all scattered throughout the Great Canon.
Now, the titles of the scriptures and their case numbers are recorded here to facilitate easy consultation.

*The Buddha-Spoken Sutra on the Immeasurable Pure and Equal Enlightenment*, one volume in two fascicles; translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Lokakṣema of the Yuezhi during the Later Han Dynasty; contained in the "Nai" (乃) case. *Immeasurable Pure and Equal Enlightenment*.
This is an alternative name for Amitāyus Buddha.
The four characters "Pure," "Equal," and "Life" (śū) convey the meaning of the word "Amitāyus.
"Awakened" (jue) is the Chinese translation for "Buddha."

The *Sukhāvatīvyūha Sūtra* (The Buddha-spoken Amitābha Sūtra), one work in two fascicles; translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Zhi Qian of Yuezhi during the Wu dynasty, contained in the Na-case. This sūtra is also titled the *Amitābhyasamyaksambuddhasarvabuddhaparivartamanuṣyadurgatipariśodhana Sūtra*.

The *Buddhabhāṣita-aparimitāyur-jñāna-sūtra*, one fascicle in two volumes; translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Kang Senghai of the Cao Wei dynasty. This sutra also has a version translated by Zhu Fahu during the Yongjia era of the Jin dynasty.
It is currently missing from the Tibetan canon.
The "Large Version" (*Daban*) referred to in Tiantai’s commentary on the *Sukhāvatīvyūha-sūtra* is precisely the one translated by Dharmarakṣa.

The Great Treasure Accumulation Sutra, Assembly on the Tathāgata Amitāyus, Scroll Seventeen and Eighteen, Volume "Shi" (師), translated by the Tripitaka Master Bodhiruci of the Great Tang. This comprises the forty-nine assemblies of the *Ratnakūṭa*, the comprehensive Vaipulya Mahāyāna sutras.
The seventh is the *Amitāyus-parivarta*.

The Buddha’s *Mahāyāna-ameyavyūha-sūtra* in one fascicle and three volumes, translated by the Tripitaka Master Dharmabhadra of the Western Heaven during the Great Song Dynasty under imperial decree. The above constitutes five sūtras.
The *Pingdengjue* (Samantabhadra) and the *Amiduo* (Amitābha) both translated the twenty-four vows of the Bhikṣu Dharmākara;
these are found in the *Wuliangshou jing* (Sukhāvatīvyūha-sūtra) and the *Dabaoji jing* (Ratnakūṭa-sūtra).
Thus, the Forty-Eight Vows were translated.
There exists a single-text edition titled *The Sutra of the Forty-Eight Vows*, in one fascicle.
This was extracted from the *Sukhāvatīvyūha-sūtra* and does not exist as a separate text.
Furthermore, there is the *Sukhāvatīvyūha-vyūha-sūtra*.
It translates thirty-one vows.
The *Fuxing* (Subcommentary) states:
"The differences in the number of vows arise from distinct scriptural traditions and divergent views; there is no need to reconcile them."
However, upon reading the Five Classics closely,
it appears that their general structure from beginning to end is identical,
as if they were derived from the same Sanskrit original.
It is merely a difference in the translators;
the detailed or abbreviated versions are simply according to what is appropriate. Yet, Jingxi said:
As for the differences in schools and divergent views,
this reveals that the Buddha’s teachings are identical in essence, yet differ according to the varying capacities of sentient beings.
As for the matters of compilation and translation, these differ in every case.
Thus, regarding the arguments concerning their similarities and differences, I do not venture to reach a definitive judgment; let the reader examine them in detail.
Among the five translations,
the textual characteristics of the Cao Wei version are particularly clear; for this reason, I have adopted it.
The various writings of the Patriarchs frequently cite this work.

*The Sutra Spoken by the Buddha on Amitābha*, one fascicle; translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Kumārajīva of the Yao Qin dynasty during the Yang period; contained in the Yao section of the canon. *The Commentary on the Contemplation Sutra* by Tiantai.
This sutra is designated as the "Shorter Version," while the previously mentioned *Sukhāvatīvyūha Sūtra* is the "Longer Version.
[The third is] the *Amitāyurdhyāna Sūtra*.
Situated between two sutras, its meaning accords with the *Madhyamāgama*.

*The Sutra on Praising the Pure Land and Being Received by the Buddha*, one fascicle; translated by the Tripitaka Master Xuanzang of the Great Tang. The above two sutras are different translations of the same original text.
The Qin edition lists the praises of the Buddhas of the six directions,
whereas the Tang translation includes the praises of the Buddhas of the ten directions;
this too is due to the translators.
The expansion and abbreviation [of the text] vary according to the occasion.
Regarding the *Longshu Jingtuwen* (Pure Land Text of Longshu),
it states that those who claim the Qin edition omits the four directions do not understand [the matter].
This is a section of the Translation Department.

*The Sutra Spoken by the Buddha on the Visualization of the Buddha of Immeasurable Life*, one fascicle; translated by Jñānagupta during the Yuanjia era of the Song dynasty, contained in the box marked with the character "Yang. This is a single-text version of the sutra; there is no duplicate translation preserved in the canon.
Also titled *The Sūtra on Purifying Karmic Obstacles and Being Born Before All Buddhas*.
Later: *The One-Scroll Sūtra of Verses on Amitābha Buddha*, translated during the Later Han dynasty (translator lost). This sūtra consists solely of fifty-six lines of verse.
The literary style of these dharma discourses is concise and archaic;
it is impossible for those of ancient or modern times to evaluate them.

*The One-Scroll Sutra of the Dharani of the King of Amitābha’s Drum Sound* (1 scroll), contained in the section labeled "Lao" (羔), is of lost translation. These two aforementioned sutras are designated as works of lost translation.
The name of the translator was also lost. There are those who,
not understanding this, claim that "lost translation" refers to a work whose translator's name was not translated [recorded].
Those not translated are in Sanskrit script.

*Pratyutpanna-buddha-saṃmukhāvasthita-samādhi-sūtra*, one volume in three fascicles; translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Lokakṣema of the Yuezhi during the Later Han dynasty. Within this collection are also the *Mahāvaipulya Mahāsaṃnipāta Bhadrapāla-parivarta Sūtra* and the *Bhadrapāla Sūtra*.
This is a different translation of the same original text as the *Pratyutpanna-samādhi-sūtra*.
It exclusively explains the samādhi in which all Buddhas of the present stand before one;
for ninety days, one contemplates and recites the name of Amitābha.

The *Mahā-śamatha-vipaśyanā* (Mohe zhiguan) is based upon the *Sūtra on the Most Victorious Dhāraṇī of the Tathāgata’s Uṣṇīṣa*, one fascicle, translated by the Tripitaka Master Dharmadeva of India during the reign of Emperor Taizong of the Great Song Dynasty, as commissioned by imperial decree. This sūtra concerns Amitāyus Buddha.
It is taught that by reciting this dhāraṇī for the sake of sentient beings, their lifespan shall be extended, and at the end of life, they will immediately attain rebirth in Sukhāvatī.

*The Ritual Manual for the Cultivation of Contemplation and Offerings to the Tathāgata Amitāyus*, one fascicle; translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Amoghavajra of Daxingshan Monastery under imperial decree, contained in the section marked with the character "Héng. This is the ritual manual.
One constructs a ritual altar and recites mantras, single-mindedly aspiring for rebirth [in the Pure Land].
*The Treatise on the Upadeśa of Amitāyus*, one fascicle; composed by the Bodhisattva Vāsuludhu; contained in the Tang section.
Translated by the Indian Tripiṭaka Master Bodhiruci during the Northern Wei dynasty. "Vasubandhu" is translated here as "Heavenly Friend" (Tiānqīn).
This is the very same *Treatise on Rebirth* (*Wǎngshēng lùn*) referred to in Tiantai’s *Ten Doubts* (*Shíyí lùn*).
This treatise comprehensively extends to all the various Pure Land sutras;
it may serve as a great aid for those capable of contemplation in their pure practices.
Regarding the *Biography of the Inconceivable Spiritual Power of the Amitābha Sūtra* (contained in the Yang section), this biography lacks the name of its author.
In the same volume as the *Smaller Amitābha Sūtra*, it contains the *Mantra for Rebirth*.
*Collection of Rituals for Liturgy and Repentance According to Various Sūtras*, two volumes; upper volume of the "Qun" (群) case, compiled by the Tang Dynasty śramaṇa Zhisheng.
The first half of this volume universally pays homage to all Buddhas;
the second half specifically contains verses for the worship and praise of the Western [Pure Land],
as well as texts for repentance and the making of vows.
The lower volume contains the Bhikṣu Shandao’s *Essential Meaning of Single-minded Cultivation of the Western Pure Land* with his own annotations and selections,
as well as a compilation of the hymns for the six periods of worship and praise for the Pure Land by various patriarchs.
The above sixteen types of sutras, śāstras, and biographies are all exclusively devoted to discussing the Pure Land. Therefore,
the *Ten Doubts Treatise* states:
In the Tibetan canon, there are more than several dozen sūtras and śāstras that earnestly instruct and exhort one to be reborn in the Western Land;
it was only the former sages who claimed there were merely seven sūtras concerning the Pure Land.
Is this not clear?
Regarding the beginning of the conditions for transformation within the traces of Amitābha in the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, the "Parable of the Phantom City" chapter states:
In the past, there was a Buddha named Mahābhijñājñānābhibhū.
Before that Buddha had left the household life, he...
He had sixteen sons,
all of whom left home as youths to become śrāmaṇeras.
At that time, that Buddha...
Having spoken this sutra,
he immediately entered a quiet chamber for eighty-four thousand kalpas.
At that time, the sixteen bodhisattvas...
Knowing that the Buddha had entered the room,
they each ascended their Dharma seats for the sake of the fourfold assembly.
In detailing the exposition of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*,
each of them delivered six hundred and eighty million *nayuta* of sentient beings, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges River;
these were the sentient beings converted by those sixteen bodhisattvas.
In birth after birth, they have been born together with the Bodhisattva.
These sixteen śrāmaṇeras are currently preaching the Dharma in the ten directions.
It continues, saying:
"In the western direction, there are two Buddhas;
one is named Amitābha."
I, Śākyamuni, am the sixteenth; at that time, you bhikṣus were the sentient beings whom I transformed.
These are the śrāvaka disciples who will exist in future ages after my parinirvāṇa.
When the Tathāgata knows for himself that the time for his nirvāṇa has arrived,
he then assembles the assembly of bodhisattvas and śrāvakas.
In expounding this sutra, the Tiantai school elucidates the "Original and Traced" (ben-ji) aspects of the Lotus Sutra; within the traced aspect,
the Great Pervasive King (Mahābhijñājñānābhibhū) is taken as the primary figure.
This passage contains three intended meanings:

first, the initial formation of karmic connections, from the section beginning with "At that time, the sixteen bodhisattvas..."; second, the intermediate meeting and encounter, from the section beginning with "These sixteen bodhisattvas..."; and third, the preaching of the Lotus Sūtra today, from the section beginning with "If the Tathāgata...". These three points collectively encompass the entirety of his manifested traces throughout this single period of his life in the other world.
As it was with Śākyamuni,
so it is with Amitābha;
this is truly because of the sixteen princes.
During the time of the Great Pervasion,
he gave a supplementary lecture to establish karmic connections for sentient beings; as for those princes—
Each attained Buddhahood;
in the Western Quarter he is known as Amitābha.
Judging the cause by the fruit, one may understand this.
At that time, Amitābha was the ninth prince;
he expounded the teachings for the multitude.
Thus it is known.
It is clear that Amitābha formed karmic affinities for sentient beings.
Thus, the *Miaoxuan* (Profound Meaning), fascicle six, states:
"The Great Universal Wisdom King was the first to form affinities for the Mahāyāna."
That Buddha preached the sutra for eight thousand kalpas,
and the sixteen princes expounded it again for eighty-four thousand kalpas;
at that time, the assembly of listeners—
This means that some may attain awakening while seated,
some may enter [the path] midway,
and others may attain it only when they are close to being transformed. This is the intended meaning.
By weighing and evaluating in this manner, it is revealed not only that the Buddhas are identical in the way they bestow their transformative teachings,
but it also allows one to know [this].
Those who have been born in the Pure Land from antiquity until the present were all members of the assembly with whom the Ninth Prince established karmic connections at that time.

*The Sutra of the Compassionate Lotus* (Beihua jing): "The Prophecy of the Names Based on the Vows of the Causes and Conditions of the Three Holy Ones. Long ago, past incalculable eons (*asaṃkhyeya-kalpa*) as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, there was a world.
The name of the kalpa was Saṃdara,
and its eon was named Susthita;
there was a wheel-turning monarch.
He was named Araṇemin and ruled over the four continents.
He had a chief minister.
His name was Ratnasāgara.
He was born into a lineage of brahmins,
and at birth he possessed the thirty-two marks and eighty minor characteristics of a great man.
His constant radiance extends one fathom;
at the time of his birth, hundreds of thousands of devas come together to make offerings.
Because he performed this writing,
he was named Ratnagarbha (Treasure Store).
Subsequently, he left the household life.
Having shaved off his beard and hair,
he attained the path to Bodhi and was again named Ratnagarbha.
The Tathāgata extensively expounded the True Dharma for the noble king.

This is the retribution of the Buddha’s Dharma-nature body.
When the minds of sentient beings are pure,
the Dharma-body is sovereign.
Therefore, it is said that he "enters.
It is like the white sun ascending into heaven, its reflection appearing in a hundred rivers;
this clarifies that the Buddha-body is sovereign and capable of manifesting in accordance with sentient beings.
Furthermore, the body of the dharma-realm is the Buddha-body;
there is nowhere it does not pervade,
and the dharma-realm constitutes its essence.
Having attained this Samādhi of Contemplating the Buddha,
one understands and enters into its corresponding application;
therefore, it is said that one enters the mental image.
As for "this mind makes the Buddha," it is because the Buddha is fundamentally non-existent that he exists through purity.
As for "this mind is the Buddha,"...
Previously, when it was asked that the Buddha is fundamentally non-existent because he is pure,
one then spoke of them as being distinct;
therefore, it is said that they are identical.
What begins as learning is called "practice";
what culminates in completion is "attainment.
The *Miaozong* commentary explains:
If one wishes to contemplate the Buddha-body,

This essence is original enlightenment, which arises and functions as the capacity for contemplation.
Original enlightenment (prakṛtistha-gotra) is the body of the dharma-dhātu of all Buddhas,

From "the body of the dharma-realm" downward,

Just as a finger does not touch itself and a blade does not cut itself, so it is with the Pratyutpanna Samādhi:

It is because the Tathāgata feared that people would become attached to signs when contemplating the Buddha.
Before the true image,
demonstrate the essence of contemplation,

Therefore, the Buddha’s manifest knowledge of the luminous nature of the fundamental substance is established by relying on external objects as its meaning and is founded upon the contemplation of "mind-only."

This is because the acts of refuting and establishing are termed "making."
The two contemplations of emptiness and conventionality;

When it is entirely "is" while acting,
then the three truths are simultaneously negated and simultaneously established;
when it is entirely acting while being "is."

they function as the emptiness, the provisional, and the middle,
capable of destroying the three delusions.

one brings about the perfect response of the three bodies of other Buddhas,

That which is designated as the middle between emptiness and the provisional is precisely this:

and the entirety of hindrances is itself virtue.
Therefore, the mind is the Responsive Buddha (yingshengfo) and the mind is the Fruitional Buddha (guofo).
Thus one should know:
by practicing these three contemplations with single-minded concentration, one attains this.

This meaning applies throughout from beginning to end;

One must not fail to know this.

even down to a single thought-moment, without harboring any doubt.

Whatever roots of goodness one performs,
one dedicates them all toward rebirth [in the Pure Land].
Therefore, it is called the mind of dedication and aspiration.
Possessing these three minds,
one will certainly attain birth [in that realm].
If even one thought-moment is lacking, rebirth cannot be attained.

Regarding those who attain rebirth in the lowest grade of the lowest class:
Having committed unwholesome deeds— the five heinous crimes and the ten evil acts—
one ought to fall into the evil realms because of those evil karmas.
When such a foolish person approaches the end of life,
they may encounter a virtuous friend who explains the sublime Dharma and instructs them to practice mindfulness of the Buddha.
This person, oppressed by suffering,
has no leisure to mindfully recite the Buddha's name.
A virtuous friend says to them:
If you are unable to maintain mindfulness,
you should recite the name of Amitāyus Buddha;
do so with such single-minded devotion that the sound does not cease.
Possessing ten recitations,
one invokes the name of Namu Amida Butsu; by virtue of invoking the Buddha's name,
[one attains birth in the Pure Land].
In every thought-moment,
one eliminates the sins of birth and death accumulated over eighty billion kalpas.
At the time of death, [one will...]
Upon seeing the golden lotus flower,
one immediately attains rebirth there.
The *Commentary on the Contemplation Sutra* states:
The continuity of the wholesome mind extends to ten recitations; or,

A question is raised: how can the power of the mind for such a short duration overcome the evil committed throughout an entire lifetime?

its power is fierce and sharp, and it resolutely determines the truth.
This power of aspiration surpasses that of a hundred years;

It is like a person who enters the ranks of battle without sparing their own life; such a person is called a hero.
The Miaozong says:
"Although this person commits evil,..."
Because they have already practiced contemplation,
when exhorted to mindfulness at the time of death,
their concentrated mind will be perfected.
They are also people whose aspiration for the vehicle is swift while their observance of the precepts is lax.

it is because seeds planted in the past have now ripened.
Therefore, the *Ten Doubts Treatise* (*Shiyi lun*) states:

having now encountered a spiritual friend,
this explanation has been composed.

From the *Sukhāvatīvyūha Sūtra*: "When these words were spoken, all the ladies-in-waiting of Vaidehī attained rebirth [in the Land of Utmost Bliss]."
When Vaidehī and her five hundred attendants heard what the Buddha had said,
they immediately beheld the world of Ultimate Bliss at that very moment.
Their hearts were filled with joy, and they attained the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharmakṣānti*).
The World-Honored One bestowed predictions upon them all.
"All shall be reborn there.

this [statement] was made in reference to them.
Those born in that land have pure faculties and are free from desire; therefore, there are no women.
Their physical faculties are supremely refined.
Therefore, there are no deficiencies of the sense faculties.
Because the scriptural passage refers to those who are newly born,
those with virtuous minds can all go there.
The *Ten Doubts Treatise* (*Shiyi lun*) states:

According to the *Sukhāvatīvyūha Sūtra*, those who give rise to a doubting mind will be born on the outskirts of the Western Realm. As for those of middle capacity mentioned in the *Amitābha Sūtra*, the Buddha said: [The Buddha said: "Among them, those of middle capacity..."

If one regrets it in the midst of human affairs,
harbors doubt in one's heart,

such a person continues their recitation without interruption,

Regarding the hearing of the sutras and the understanding thereof:

Great joy arose within his heart,
and he thought to himself:
"I regret that I did not realize how much benefit there is in performing various wholesome deeds."
Now they shall be reborn there;
those people merely contemplate [the Buddha] with their minds,
for they are unable to speak with their mouths.
As for those who immediately repent their transgressions,
their doubts may be somewhat diminished;
yet if they do not repent, it will be of no avail.
When that person’s life comes to an end,
they will be reborn in the land of Amitābha Buddha; however,
they will not be able to go there immediately.
He then saw a city of seven treasures extending for two thousand li;
his heart was filled with solitary joy,
and he stayed within it.
In bathing pools of the seven treasures,
they are born by transformation from lotus flowers,
like the spontaneous objects found in the second heaven, the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven.
After five hundred years within that city have passed,
he is finally able to emerge and reach the presence of Amitābha Buddha;
there, the person hears the sutra.
Their minds lack understanding,
their wisdom is not clear,
and the dwellings where they reside are upon the earth.
They cannot cause their dwellings to rise as high or large as they wish within the void;
furthermore, they remain very far from Amitābha Buddha and are unable to draw near.
It is also like the second case of those of middling capacity who harbor doubts;
after a long time, their wisdom shall likewise open and resolve,
and they will come to know the sutras with vigor.
Next, they are as described for the first class above.
Why is this? It is because they all sat [in meditation] during their previous lives when they were seeking the Way.
They feel regret and doubt in their hearts;
they believe for a moment and then do not believe for a moment.
They do not believe that by performing good deeds one obtains meritorious blessings.
All of these are obtained spontaneously;
one should know that those who give rise to doubt and confusion [fail to realize this].
This results in the loss of great benefit.
Therefore, one should clearly believe in and understand the unsurpassed wisdom of all Buddhas.
The *Commentary on the Sutra of Contemplation* (Guanjing shu), in its explanation of the "Contemplation of the Sun," states:
The teaching commands correct contemplation in order to eliminate doubt;
the Great Root Text clarifies that one may cultivate all merits with a mind of doubt.
Because one would fall into a borderland and further undergo birth from a womb;
by performing this contemplation, one causes such doubts to be eliminated.
*Miaozong* says:
The Sūtra says:
"If one does not understand the Buddha’s wisdom, then doubt and confusion will arise.
The Commentary says:
Therefore, this contemplation is formulated to eliminate doubt;
it is precisely to manifest this contemplation [that it is stated].
One can comprehend the Buddha’s wisdom;
if one does not employ the three contemplations to observe the setting sun,
then one will be deluded regarding the Buddha’s wisdom.
Since this is the case for the visualization of the sun,
the same principle applies to the other visualizations; thus, we know.
The Great Master, relying upon the Buddha’s wisdom, established this present method of contemplation.
Whether it be the minor virtues of ordinary beings or even those who commit various evils while dedicating [their merit] toward the Buddha’s wisdom at the time of death,
they must rely upon the Buddha’s wisdom to seek the extinction of their karmic obstacles and hindrances.
Since they possess the seeds of the vehicle to be born there,
they will swiftly behold the Triple Gem and will not be reborn in borderlands or from a womb.
From the *Bodhisattva-utkṣepa-garbha-sūtra*: "If one gives rise to a mind of defiled attachment, one will fall into the Land of Indolence. The Buddha said:
Beyond this, twelve billion nayutas of lands to the west, there is the land of Śithilamati (the Land of Indolence).
It is resolutely joyful and peaceful.
Those who wish to be reborn in the land of Amitābha Buddha [should proceed].
If one passes through this land and many people there are stained by attachment,
one immediately vows to be reborn therein.
Consequently, one will not be able to reach the land of Amitābha Buddha.
If a person sees this and neither covets nor clings to it, [they shall attain rebirth].
One will immediately transcend [this realm] and reach the Land of Peace and Bliss.
The *Commentary on the Amitābha Sūtra* states:
"This is the Land of Indolence."
This refers to what is called the "City of Doubt" in the *Sukhāvatīvyūha Sūtra*.
Fearing that sentient beings might harbor doubts while recollecting the Buddha,
the Buddha manifested this land.
Question: Since it is said that it is "lazy and indolent," how can there be happiness?
Answer: If contrasted with the Land of Ultimate Bliss (Sukhāvatī), it is considered lazy and indolent.
If one faces the Sahā world, it is itself happiness.

*The Scripture on Equal Enlightenment*: Regarding the realization of the fruits of the practice of Śrāvakas in the Pure Land, the Infinite Purity Buddha-land. *The Scripture on Equal Enlightenment*: Regarding the realization of the fruits of the practice of Śrāvakas in the Pure Land, the Infinite Purity Buddha-land.
Those various bodhisattvas and arhats each practiced their own paths; among them,
some were on the ground expounding the sutras.
Among those who recite the sutras and practice seated meditation,
there are some who preach and practice the sutras while suspended in mid-air;
among them, there are those who have not yet attained the stage of Srotāpanna.

Then those who had not yet attained the path of the Srotāpanna would attain the path of the Srotāpanna; those who had not yet attained the path of the Sakṛdāgāmin would attain the path of the Sakṛdāgāmin.

those who have not yet attained the path of arhat shall [attain the path of arhat].
Then those who have attained the path of Arhatship shall remain so;
those who have not yet attained the stage of Avaivartika shall attain the stage of Avaivartika.
Each person practicing the Way does so with joy.
Furthermore, the *Sukhāvatīvyūha Sūtra* states:
The disciples of that Buddha are all arhats;
they cannot be reckoned by calculation.

The *Ten Doubts Treatise* says:
He possesses no mind for the two vehicles;
he is a purely Mahāyāna, pure, and excellent companion.
The *Commentary on the Contemplation Sūtra* asks:
According to the *Wangsheng lun* (Treatise on Rebirth), those of the two vehicles are not born [in the Pure Land].
Yet, in the *Guan jing* (Contemplation Sutra), it is said that those of the middle grade who follow the Small Vehicle can attain birth; how is this so?
Answer: It is not produced through minor practices in the right circumstances;
rather, it is only by generating the seeds of the Mahāyāna at the point of death that one can attain birth [in that realm].
Because they had previously studied the Hinayana extensively,
upon hearing of suffering, emptiness, and impermanence there,
their original understanding was awakened.
They first realize the small fruit;
having attained the small fruit,
they do not abide in that which is small.
"One must necessarily return and enter the Great [Vehicle]. Miaozong said:
"Because they turn their minds [toward enlightenment], they attain birth [in that realm]."
Due to habituation, one realizes the small;
knowing the great, one realizes the small.
One does not cling to partial truth as the ultimate.
Before long, one will realize the Great [Enlightenment].

*The Sutra of Immeasurable Life*: Regarding the exclusion of those who commit the five heinous crimes or slander the Dharma from attaining rebirth in the Land of Immeasurable Life, the eighteenth of the Forty-eight Vows states:
If, when I attain Buddhahood,
the sentient beings of the ten directions should,
with a sincere heart, believe and rejoice;
If those who desire to be born in my land—
even those with as few as ten recitations— should not be born there, [may I not attain perfect enlightenment].
"I shall not attain perfect enlightenment,
except for those who commit the five heinous crimes or slander the true Dharma.
Furthermore, the lower fascicle states:
All those who hear the name of the Buddha and,
with faith and joy, [contemplate it] for even a single thought-moment.
If one makes the vow for rebirth through dedication, one will immediately attain rebirth,
with the sole exception of those who have committed the five heinous crimes or slandered the True Dharma.
The *Commentary on the Sutra of Contemplation* states:

In the *Mahāvaipulya Sūtra*, it is taught that those who commit the five heinous crimes or slander the Dharma cannot be reborn [in the Pure Land]. Yet, in this *Contemplation Sūtra*, it is said that even those with such heinous offenses may attain rebirth.
There are two interpretations for this.
Regarding the commission of offenses by persons, there are superior and inferior degrees.
One of superior faculties, such as King Ajātaśatru who committed a parricidal offense,
will necessarily experience profound remorse.
This causes their offenses to be diminished and thinned,
allowing them to attain rebirth.
Those of inferior faculties who commit acts of immediate retribution generally lack profound remorse.
Therefore, it cannot arise.
Second, regarding practice:
practice may be either concentrated or dispersed.
The Samādhi of Contemplating the Buddha is called concentration;
cultivating other wholesome karmas is termed distraction.
The power of distracted goodness is slight.
Those who do not eliminate the five grave offenses shall not attain rebirth there;
this is the conclusion of the Great Sutra.
Therefore, it is said that there is no birth.
This sutra clarifies contemplation, and thus speaks of attaining birth.
*The Sutra of Immeasurable Life*—the marks of rebirth through the cultivation of causes by the three grades. The Buddha said:
Sentient beings of the ten directions who wish to be born in that land are divided into three grades.
As for those of the highest grade:
Having left home and renounced desire,
he became a śramaṇa and gave rise to the bodhicitta.
One should single-mindedly and exclusively keep Amitāyus Buddha in mind,
cultivate various meritorious virtues,
and vow to be born in that land.
When this person's life comes to an end,
Amitāyus Buddha, together with a great multitude,
will appear before them.
He immediately followed that Buddha,
being born within a flower made of the seven treasures,
and dwelt in the stage of non-retrogression.
Possessing wisdom and valor,
with sovereign mastery of supernatural powers—
such are those of the middle grade.
One should sincerely wish to be born in that land;
even if one does not become a śramaṇa,
one should extensively cultivate meritorious deeds.
One should resolve to attain unsurpassed bodhicitta and single-mindedly and exclusively keep Amitāyus Buddha in mind,
performing as much wholesome practice as possible.
They uphold the precepts of fasting and purification;
they erect stupas and images;
and they provide food for śramaṇas and others.
Dedicating these merits, they vow to be born in that land.
At the time of their death,
Amitāyus Buddha will manifest his transformed body before them.
Together with the great assembly, he appeared before that person;
immediately following the transformation Buddha, he was reborn in that land and dwelt in the stage of non-retrogression.
Those with merit and wisdom constitute the middle class.
As for those of the lower class,
they desire with a sincere heart to be born in that land.
Even if one has not performed any meritorious deeds,
one should resolve upon the unsurpassed mind of enlightenment and focus the mind single-mindedly for as few as ten recitations.
If one hears this profound Dharma and,
with joy and faith, does not give rise to doubt or confusion,
but even for a single moment of thought brings that Buddha to mind.
When this person was approaching death,
they dreamed of that Buddha and likewise attained rebirth there.
In terms of merit and wisdom, this is the middle grade.
The *Commentary on the Contemplation Sutra* states:
"The *Contemplation Sutra* has nine grades."
This is to establish the superior, middling, and inferior grades within the stage of consciousness;
these correspond precisely to the three categories of the *Mūla-śāstra*.
The *Gushan Kuanzheng Ji* states:
The three grades in the *Mūla-sūtra* correspond only to the six chapters of the *Contemplation Sūtra*,
for those three grades exclusively clarify virtuous conduct.
This is because they do not fall into the ranks of the wicked.
Lingzhi states that there are three grades in the Great Text.
All of them have previously awakened the aspiration;
this corresponds to the superior grade of the *Amitābha Sūtra*, while the middle and lower grades correspond to the middle and lower grades [of the *Sukhāvatīvyūha Sūtra*].
This is not what is being addressed;
how much less so when the causal practice is entirely different from the present one.
The *Fuzhengjie* (Exposition on Aiding Correct Understanding) states:
Tiantai takes the nine grades of the present sutra and correlates them with the three ranks of the Larger Sutra;
he does so by correlating them based on the fact that their respective stages and levels are identical.
This does not correlate the three grades by means of the characteristics of the resolve generated through the causes of practice.
In the *Sūtra of Immeasurable Life*, regarding the comparison of the differences in the cultivation of goodness in the two lands, the Buddha said:
People of later generations who obtain the words of the Buddha’s sutras should reflect upon them thoroughly;
they will then be able to [understand] within them.
With a focused mind and upright conduct,
he takes the initiative to perform good deeds and leads those beneath him through transformation.
They exhorted one another in turn,
each maintaining steadfast composure and extensively cultivating the roots of virtue.
Practicing generosity and bestowing kindness;
practicing patience and diligence;
and cultivating single-minded concentration and wisdom.
With a rectified mind and rectified intent,
observe the fast and maintain purity for one day and one night;
this is superior to practicing virtue for a hundred years in the Land of Immeasurable Life.
Why is this? Because that Buddha-land is unconditioned and spontaneous,
being entirely accumulated through manifold virtues.
There is no evil of even a hair’s breadth here;
therefore, practicing virtue for ten days and ten nights here is superior to practicing virtue for a thousand years in the Buddha-fields of other directions.
This is because in other Buddha-lands, those who do good are many and those who do evil are few;
only here is there so much evil that there is no spontaneity.
Your minds are exhausted and your bodies are weary;
you drink bitterness and consume poison.
I have compassion for you all.
With great effort, he instructed and exhorted them, teaching them to cultivate goodness.

In the *Sūtra of Immeasurable Life*, there are many bodhisattvas who have attained rebirth in the Pure Land. Maitreya addressed the Buddha, saying: [In the *Sūtra of Immeasurable Life*, there are many bodhisattvas who have attained rebirth in the Pure Land.]
"In this world, how many non-retrogressive bodhisattvas are reborn in Sukhāvatī?
The Buddha told Maitreya:
In this world, there are sixty-seven billion non-retrogressive bodhisattvas who will be reborn in that land.
Each and every bodhisattva has already made offerings to countless buddhas,
just as Maitreya has done.
The number of bodhisattvas who practice minor deeds,
as well as those who cultivate meager merit,
is beyond measure and calculation.
All shall attain rebirth there.
Furthermore, it is not only the bodhisattvas of my own land who will attain rebirth,
but also those from the buddha-fields of other directions.
In the Buddha-field of Dūraprāśa,
there are eighteen billion bodhisattvas who shall all be reborn there.
Not only do bodhisattvas from these fourteen buddha-fields attain rebirth there;
those who attain rebirth in the immeasurable buddha-fields throughout the worlds of the ten directions are even more numerous and incalculable.
If I were to explain it in full detail,
even an entire eon would not suffice;
now I have merely spoken of it in brief.
*The Sutra of Immeasurable Life: A Sutra Remaining After the Extinction of the Dharma for a Hundred Years to Deliver Innumerable People*. If there are those who hear this sutra...
One shall never regress from the unsurpassed path; therefore,
one should practice with single-minded devotion.
I shall preach this sutra-dharma so that you may behold Amitāyus Buddha and his land; this is what must be done.
All these may be sought therein.
Do not allow yourselves to give rise to further doubt and confusion after my parinirvāṇa.
In future ages, [you shall find them there].
When the teachings of the sutras have been extinguished, I shall, out of compassion,
specially preserve this sutra.
It shall remain for a hundred years.
Any sentient beings who encounter this sutra will all attain liberation according to their wishes.
Those who do not believe in, praise, or extol the name of Amitābha Buddha, but instead slander and revile it,
shall fall into hell for five kalpas and undergo all manner of suffering there.
The Sūtra of Immeasurable Life: Exhorting All to Strive Diligently to Seek It. The Buddha addressed Maitreya:
The various devas and humans [in] the Land of Immeasurable Life are subtle,
wondrous, peaceful, and blissful.
Purity is such as this;
why not exert yourself to do good?
Contemplate the spontaneity of the Way.
Abiding in that which is neither above nor below,
penetrating to the boundless limits—
one should each exert oneself with diligent vigor.
Strive to seek it for yourself;
you will surely attain transcendence and be reborn in the Land of Peaceful Nurturing.
Transversely cutting off the five evil paths,
the miserable realms naturally close;
ascending the Way, there is no end.
It is easy to go, yet no one does;
their land does not oppose or resist.
It is that which is naturally drawn forth.
Why not abandon worldly affairs and diligently practice to seek the Way and its Virtue?
Thus one may attain ultimate longevity.
Life and happiness are without limit.
*The Sutra of Immeasurable Life*. *The Sutra of the Universal Radiance of the Buddha of Immeasurable Life*. The Buddha addressed Ānanda:
The Buddha of Immeasurable Life possesses majestic spiritual power and radiance that is most honored and supreme.
The radiance of all Buddhas cannot reach it; there may even be some Buddha-radiance that [cannot reach it].
It illuminates a hundred Buddha-worlds,
or a thousand Buddha-worlds; to speak in brief:
It then illuminated Buddha-fields as numerous as the sands of the Ganges in the eastern direction;
the same was likewise true for the south, west, north, the four intermediate directions, and the zenith and nadir.
There may be Buddha-radiance that illuminates seven feet,
or it may illuminate one yojana.
In this manner, it increases twofold at each stage until it illuminates a single buddha-field;
therefore, [he is called] Amitāyus Buddha.
They are named Buddha Immeasurable Light,
Buddha Boundless Light,
Buddha Unobstructed Light, and so forth.
Any sentient beings who encounter this light will have their three defilements extinguished,
and their bodies and minds will become supple and gentle.
They will feel joyful and exultant,
and wholesome thoughts will arise within them,
even if they are currently in the three miserable realms.
Upon seeing this radiance,
they will no longer experience suffering or affliction.
After their lives come to an end, [they shall attain rebirth].
All receive liberation.

In the *Sukhāvatīvyūha Sūtra*: "In that Buddha-land, precious bowls and food and drink are spontaneously filled to overflowing. In the *Sukhāvatīvyūha Sūtra*: "In that Buddha-land, precious bowls and food and drink are spontaneously filled to overflowing."
For all those who are reborn there, palaces,
clothing, and precious vessels appear spontaneously before them.
Bowl-sets made of gold, silver,
and lapis lazuli arrived at will,
along with food and drink of a hundred flavors.
It becomes naturally full;
although this food exists,
there is in fact no one who eats it.
They merely see forms and smell fragrances;
their minds take these as food,
and they are naturally satisfied.
With body and mind supple and pliant,
he was free from all attachment;
having completed his task, he vanished.
When the time arrives, they appear once more.
Furthermore, both the *Fǎděngjué jīng* (Sūtra of the Awakening of Equality) and the *Dà āmítuó jīng* (Great Amitābha Sūtra) state:
The Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, and Arhats of Amitābha all possess natural bowls made of the seven treasures;
within these bowls are foods and drinks of a hundred flavors.
Unlike those of the mundane world or the heavens throughout the eight directions and above and below,
the refined flavors, fragrances, and tastes within their food and drink are peerless;
they are produced spontaneously through transformation.
If one desires sweet vinegar,
it shall be obtained as desired;
whatever one eats shall be neither too much nor too little.
Nor did he speak of beauty or ugliness.
Having finished eating, he vanished;
all that was consumed was pure and undefiled.
It serves merely as a source of vital energy.
The *Wangsheng lun* (Treatise on Rebirth) states:
"One cherishes and delights in the flavor of the Buddha-dharma."
The food is the samādhi of dhyāna.
The *An-yang ji* states:
"Regarding the initial statement that there is truly no food..."
The next two sūtras refer to eating for the sake of utilizing physical strength;
according to this principle, as long as one has not yet abandoned edible food in the desire realm, one must eat it.
According to the account of Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra’s attainment of Buddhahood,
he partakes of the food of Dharma-joy and the rapture of dhyāna,
having no further thought of other food.
Thus, it should be understood that even in the Pure Land, there may truly be no food; for in that land,
the four subtle elements consist of a hundred flavors.
Since these have been prepared according to one's wishes,
whether one eats them or not,
how can there be only a single course of action?
The two sūtras each provide their own account;
these are merely adaptations to the preferences of their respective times.

In the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, the "Chapter on the Lifespan" (*Āyuṣpramāṇa-parivarta*), Bodhisattva Cittarāja says, while comparing the lengths of day and night in the two lands: [The text continues with the comparison of the day and night in the two lands.]
One kalpa in the Sahā world, the buddha-field of Śākyamuni Buddha,
constitutes a single day and night in the Sukhāvatī world, the buddha-field of Amitābha Buddha.
One kalpa of the Land of Ultimate Bliss is a single day and night in the Vajra-firm Buddha-field of the world named Kāṣāyadhvaja.
Proceeding in this sequence through more than a million asaṃkhyeya worlds,
at the end of one kalpa, there was the world-realm of the Buddha Bhadraśrī in the world called Uttarakusuma.
This constitutes one day and night.
Furthermore, the *Sukhāvatīvyūha Sūtra* states:
"In that Buddha-land, there are six periods of day and night."
The *Tongzan* (General Praise) of Ci'en's [Commentary on the Amitābha Sūtra] states:
"In the Pure Land, there are six periods each for day and night.
It asks: "The people of the Pure Land are entirely devoid of ignorance."
The land has neither dawn nor dusk;
how can one speak of day and night?
Answer: Flowers bloom in the golden pond, and beings are born through transformation.
For those with the sentiment of the breaking dawn,
birds nest in the jade groves;
for the Bodhisattva, there is the thought of the darkness of night.
The *Xinshu* of Zhuchuan states:
"One should know that the 'six periods' must refer to three during the day and three during the night."
The sentient beings in that land possess radiance from their own bodies;
there is no Mount Sumeru.
One does not distinguish day and night by the rising and setting of the sun;
as stated in the *Shiqian*,
the various devas indicate day and night by the opening and closing of flowers.
Thus, the explanation of Ci'en may well be correct;
this merely borrows the divisions of time from this land to designate the temporal periods of that realm.
As stated in the Avataṃsaka Sūtra,
the six periods of the western region truly cannot be measured against the length of the local hours such as yin and mao.
Alternatively, one might not accept what Ci'en has said,
on the grounds that it lacks supporting evidence.
However, I have read the *Karunāpuṇḍarīka-sūtra*.
That world of the Buddha Padmottama is called "Ever-Luminous.
That Buddha constantly possesses radiance;
because the flowers close and the birds settle, the Bodhisattvas enter meditative concentration there.
He then knew it was the night when the wind blew the flowers away and the various birds sang together in harmony.
The Bodhisattva arose from meditative concentration and knew it was the daytime.

In the *Mañjuśrī-paripṛcchā-prajñāpāramitā-sūtra*, regarding the cultivation of the *ekavyūha-samādhi* by exclusively reciting the name of the Buddha, Mañjuśrī said: In the *Mañjuśrī-paripṛcchā-prajñāpāramitā-sūtra*, regarding the cultivation of the *ekavyūha-samādhi* by exclusively reciting the name of the Buddha, Mañjuśrī said:
"What is called the Samādhi of One Practice?
The Buddha said:
'The Dharma-realm has a single characteristic; one binds the conditions of mindfulness to the Dharma-realm.'"
This is called the Samādhi of One Practice.
Those who wish to enter the Samādhi of One Practice should dwell in a secluded and quiet place.
Abandon all distracted thoughts;
do not grasp at appearances,
but bind the mind to a single Buddha.
Single-mindedly reciting the name,
following the direction of the Buddha,
with body upright and facing forward.
One is able, with respect to a single Buddha,
to maintain a continuous succession of thoughts;
within these very thoughts, [one practices].
One is able to see all Buddhas of the past and present.
Why is this? Because by recollecting the merit of a single Buddha, [one sees them all].
Furthermore, they are non-dual with the merits of immeasurable Buddhas;
all become one suchness and attain supreme perfect enlightenment.
The *Tiantai Zhiguan* states:
"The Samādhi of Constant Sitting is derived from the *Mañjuśrī-paripṛcchā-sūtra* (the Sūtra Spoken by Mañjuśrī on the Questions of Mañjuśrī)."
This is called the Samādhi of One Practice. For a period of ninety days,
one should sit upright with legs crossed.
Facing a particular direction toward a Buddha,
sit upright and maintain this posture continuously for a set period of time.
If one is utterly exhausted from sitting, or afflicted by illness,
or shrouded by the hindrance of drowsiness;
When internal and external obstacles invade and seize you,
you should instead single-mindedly recite the name of a single Buddha,
repenting with shame and remorse, taking refuge with your very life.
The names of the Buddhas of the ten directions are equal in merit.
The *Fuxing* (Sub-commentary) explains:
Regarding "in whichever direction of a Buddha" and so forth:
whichever direction one faces must necessarily be due west.
If obstacles arise, it is because mindfulness of the Buddha is directed toward that which is convenient.
Although the sutra does not restrict one to facing the western direction,
since it already requires the exclusive recitation of a single Buddha, [the direction follows naturally].
Since the praises found in various teachings are for the most part directed toward Amitābha,
the Western Quarter is taken as the primary standard.
As for the phrase "equal to the Buddhas of the ten directions":
This is the dispelling of doubts.
It is feared that some might wonder:
for what reason is it that one is instructed to invoke only Amitābha?
Therefore, the commentary states:
"The merits are exactly equal.
The *Pratyutpanna-samādhi Sūtra* (Banzhou jing) says: "Cultivating the Buddha-standing Samādhi and single-mindedly recollecting Amitābha Buddha. The Buddha said:
For what reason does one attain the samādhi in which all present Buddhas stand before one?
It is because there are members of the fourfold assembly who have maintained their precepts completely and dwell alone in a secluded place.
Mentally recollect Amitābha Buddha of the Western Quarter,
who currently resides one thousand million *buddhakṣetras* away from here;
his land is named Sukhāvatī.
In the midst of the assembly of bodhisattvas,
he preached the sutra, constantly keeping that Buddha in mind as if in a dream.
He saw gold, jewels, and kinsmen,
and they all enjoyed themselves together;
having awakened, he spoke of it.
If a person recollects that Buddha for one day and night,
or for more than seven days and seven nights, Amitābha Buddha—
One does not see it while awake;
one sees it in a dream when the mind forms a thought.
In all Buddha-lands,
upon the great Mount Sumeru,
and in places of profound darkness.
He opened them all up for him,
yet without employing his supernormal powers, he reached that Buddha-field while remaining right where he was.
Sitting there, he saw that Buddha and heard the sutras he preached,
just as there were three courtesans in Śrāvastī.
At that time, there were three men in the kingdom of Rājagṛha who had never before seen her;
upon hearing of her, their lustful desires were immediately stirred.
He dreamed that he went to her place and stayed with her overnight;
the act of lust was exactly as it had been.
By means of this mindfulness,
one shall see the Buddha at the time of birth;
one constantly recollects that the Buddha’s body possesses the thirty-two marks, which are upright and beyond compare.
By means of mindfulness of the Buddha,
one attains the samādhi of emptiness.
It is also like eating sweet and delicious food within a dream.
Having awakened, his belly was empty;
he thought to himself that all things possessed are like a dream.

Within samādhi, the Buddha establishes three modes of sustenance: the sustenance of the Buddha’s majestic spiritual power; the sustenance of the Buddha’s majestic spiritual power; and the sustenance of the Buddha’s majestic spiritual power. (Note: The repetition indicates the emphasis on the sustaining power of the Buddha's majesty.)
Sustained by the power of the Buddha’s samādhi and sustained by the power of one's own original merit,
it is through these three causes that one is able to see the Buddha.
He formed this thought:
"From where does the Buddha come, and to where does he go?
Reflecting upon himself, he realized that the Buddha comes from nowhere.
I, too, have nowhere to go.
What I contemplate is the seeing of the mind creating the Buddha-mind;
I see for myself that this mind is the Buddha-mind. This is it.
The Tathāgata’s mind is my own body-mind; yet when seeing the Buddha’s mind,
one does not know the mind itself.
The mind does not see itself.
When the mind has conceptualization, it is a deluded mind;
when it is without conceptualization, that is nirvana.
These dharmas have nothing in them that can be enjoyed;
they are all merely the products of thought.
Even if one were to engage in such thought, it would be nothing but emptiness.
Furthermore, there are four matters by which one quickly attains this samādhi.
The first is that one must not harbor worldly thoughts.
The first is that for three months, one must not snap one's fingers even for the duration of a finger-snap. The second is that for three months,
one must not lie down even for the duration of a finger-snap.
Third, one must not cease walking meditation;
one must not sit for three months,
except during the time immediately before and after meals.
Fourth, when preaching the sutras for others,
one must not hope for their clothing or food and drink;
this is due to the Buddha’s majestic spiritual power.
Abiding in samādhi, one beholds hundreds of thousands of Buddhas, millions of Buddhas, and billions of Buddhas in the east;
likewise, one sees all the Buddhas throughout the ten directions.
The *Zhiguan* states:
"The *Changxing Samādhi* is derived from the *Pratyutpanna Sūtra*.
'Pratyutpanna' is translated as 'the Buddha standing.'"
The Buddha’s standing has three meanings as explained in the sutra; through this samādhi it is accomplished,
whereby one is able, while in meditative concentration,
to see the Buddhas of the ten directions standing before oneself.
It is explained that there are three aspects to this samādhi:
first, the opening and closing of the body;
the opening of the body refers to constant practice.
Avoid evil associates;
always dwell in solitude;
always practice begging for food.
He did not accept separate invitations;
he adorned the site of practice and bathed his body.
Changing his robes,
he devoted himself exclusively to circumambulation for a period of ninety days.
I make this solemn vow and aspiration:
even if my sinews and bones wither and decay,
may I not attain this samādhi until I have mastered it.
He never rested. Second, regarding speech and silence:
for ninety days, his mouth constantly chanted the name of Amitābha Buddha without ceasing.
For ninety days, one should constantly and without ceasing keep Amitābha Buddha in mind.
One may practice both recitation and chanting simultaneously,
or first perform the mental recitation and subsequently engage in chanting.
Alternatively, one may chant first and then recite;
chanting and recitation follow one another in succession without a moment's rest.
If one chants the name of Amitābha,
it is equivalent to chanting the merits of the Buddhas of the ten directions;
however, Amitābha alone is designated as the presiding master of this Dharma gate.
To state the essentials:
at every step, with every sound,
and in every thought-moment, one’s focus should be solely upon Amitābha.
Third is the contemplation of mindfulness:
for three months, one constantly recollects the thirty-two marks of Amitābha,
beginning with the mark of the thousand-spoked wheel on the soles of his feet.
One should contemplate each of the marks in reverse order,
up to the invisible crown of the head;
one should likewise proceed from the crown down to the thousand-spoked wheel.
"May I also attain these marks.
Furthermore, I reflect that I shall attain Buddhahood through the mind and attain Buddhahood through the body;
yet, Buddhahood is not attained by means of the mind."
One does not attain it by means of the body,
nor does one attain the Buddha’s form by means of the mind;
one does not attain the Buddha’s mind by means of form.
The wise understand that these are fundamentally non-existent;
having destroyed the root and severed the branches, they are empty like dreaming of the seven treasures and one's kinsmen.
Having awakened, one does not know where one is.
It is like a courtesan who, having engaged in sexual intercourse in a dream at night,
remembers it upon awakening.
There is no coming and no going;
the joyful events remain vividly present,
just like dreaming of eating delicious food.
Having awakened, his stomach was empty;
he thought to himself that all existing phenomena are like dreams.
This is called mindfulness of the conventional self according to the mark of suchness:
"From where does the Buddha come? I, too, have nowhere to go.
That which I contemplate is simply the mind manifesting as the Buddha-mind."
Seeing one's own mind is seeing the Buddha-mind;
this Buddha-mind is my own mind seeing the Buddha-mind.
The mind does not know itself;
the mind does not see itself.
When the mind has conceptualization, it is a deluded mind.
Non-conception is nirvana.
This dharma cannot be demonstrated;
it is entirely the product of mental recollection.
Even if one has thoughts, they are utterly non-existent within this state. If a person wishes to attain wisdom like the great ocean and,
while seated here, desires to see all Buddhas without exercising supernatural powers, [they should practice thus].
One should cultivate this samādhi;
among all meritorious qualities, this samādhi is the most supreme.
This samādhi is the father and mother of all Buddhas;
all Tathāgatas are born from this Dharma.
The *Fuxing* (Subcommentary) explains:
Within the practice of mindfulness and contemplation,
one first takes the thirty-two marks as the object of observation.
Furthermore, I reflect that I shall now clearly illuminate the objects of perception by means of cultivating the three contemplations.
Regarding the word "Buddha" within all the phrases I have contemplated:
first, there is the Buddha seen through the samādhi of one's own mind;
second, there is the Buddha who arises from the West as the fruition resulting from causes.
Now, possessing both meanings together as a single object,
it is for the sake of conforming to the principle.
Explained according to the first meaning:
once samādhi has been accomplished,
one sees [the object] immediately upon recollecting it.
To perceive this nature of mind is called "the mind creating the Buddha.
Since the Buddha is created by the mind,
when one sees the Buddha, it is called "seeing one's own mind."
If one sees one's own mind,
one sees the Buddha-mind,
because that Buddha-mind is my own mind.
Therefore, the intention here is simply this: one contemplates only one's own mind and the Buddha as perceived,
for they do not transcend the nature of phenomena (dharmatā).
To see the Buddha’s mind is to see one’s own mind;
one’s own mind and the Buddha’s mind are precisely the Middle Way.
Regarding this, Siming Rongxin’s commentary states:
The text on the Samādhi of the Buddha’s Presence (Pratyutpanna-samādhi) as judged by Śamatha and Vipaśyanā states: that the mind and the Buddha cannot be apprehended constitutes emptiness (śūnyatā);
that dream-phenomena remain vividly present constitutes the conventional (saṃvṛti).
The mind not perceiving the mind is the Middle Way.
When explained, the three marks are distinct;
when cultivated, they are complete in a single thought-moment.
The Vaipulya Mahāsaṃnipāta Sūtra: The Method for Cultivating the Buddha-Established Samādhi and the Middle Way Contemplation. The Buddha addressed Bhadrapāla:
If one wishes to accomplish the samādhi of the presence of all Buddhas,
one will see the Tathāgata wherever one directs one's thoughts,
just as when taking clear oil, pure water, crystal, or a bright mirror.
Using these four objects to contemplate oneself as an image,
good and evil, beauty and ugliness appear with distinct clarity;
yet that manifested image—
It does not emerge from the four elements,
nor does it come from any other place;
it does not exist spontaneously.
It is not created by human hands;
you should know that the image comes from nowhere.
Furthermore, there is nowhere to which they go;
they are without arising and without cessation,
and have no place of abiding.
The Bodhisattva was likewise;
he then further reflected:
"As for this Buddha now..."
From where have they come?
And from what has this body of mine emerged?
Contemplating that Tathāgata,
one finds that he ultimately has neither place of coming nor place of going;
my own body is likewise so.
Since there is fundamentally no point of departure,
how could there be a turning back? They should further reflect in this way:
Now, these three realms exist solely as mind. Why is this?
In accordance with that thought,
one returns to seeing one's own mind;
now, following from the mind, I see the Buddha.
My mind shall become a Buddha;
my mind is a Buddha; my mind is the Tathāgata.
My mind is my body; my mind sees the Buddha.
The mind does not know the mind.
The mind does not see the mind.
When the mind possesses conceptualization,
it constitutes birth and death.
When the mind is free from conceptualization,
that is itself nirvana; once what is conceived has ceased, [nirvana is realized].
One should know that even the capacity for conceptualization is empty;
it is by means of this samādhi that a bodhisattva [proceeds].
He realized great bodhi.
This sutra is a different translation of the same original text as the aforementioned Pratyutpanna Sūtra.
The exposition of the method of contemplating the Middle Way herein is clearly articulated in its textual form; therefore,
it is recorded once more.
The Avataṃsaka Sūtra: The Chapter on the Elder Vimukta Attaining the Gate of Mind-Only Buddha-Recollection. The Elder said:
"Good son, if I wish to see the Tathāgata Amitāyus of the Land of Peace and Bliss,
I see him immediately according to my will."
In this way, if I wish to see all the Tathāgatas existing in all worlds throughout the ten directions,
I shall see them immediately according to my will.
I am able to fully comprehend all matters concerning the adornments and supernatural powers of the lands of all Tathāgatas;
they come from nowhere,
nor do they go anywhere.
There is no place of movement,
nor any place of abiding;
it is just like one's own body.
There is no coming and no going;
there is no place of movement or abiding. Yet, that Tathāgata...
They do not come here;
I do not go there. I know that all Buddhas and my own mind are one.
Because all are like dreams.
Just as what is seen in a dream arises from conceptual construction,
so too does one see all Buddhas.
It arises from one's own mind;
furthermore, one knows one's own mind to be like water in a vessel.
One realizes that all phenomena are like reflections in water,
and further understands one's own mind.
Just like a magical illusion,
one knows that all Buddhas are like what is produced by illusion.
Furthermore, one knows that one's own mind and all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas are entirely like echoes;
for example, just as an empty valley produces an echo in accordance with sound.
Having realized my own mind,
I see the Buddha through recollection;
this is how I know it.
Recalling in this way, one realizes that all the Buddhas seen arise from one's own mind;
this is from the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* translated during the Zhenyuan era.
The *Qingliang Zhenyuan Shu* states:
From "There is nowhere from which it comes" onwards, the text correctly discriminates that [all phenomena] are mind-only (*cittamātra*).
The very mind is no-mind;
thus one enters into True Suchness,
realizing that those marks are empty.
Because all is a manifestation of mind-only,
one strikes the wondrous function that is identical to its essence by means of the mind-only that is itself quiescent.
If one can maintain mindfulness in every thought-moment,
what interference could there be between movement and stillness?
Once it is realized that all is but mind alone, [delusion ceases].
Since realizing the mind is itself the Buddha,
whatever one contemplates is none other than the Buddha;
how much more so when the will is single-minded and undisturbed.
One must investigate with precision until reaching the subtlest point.
The Buddha responds according to one's sincerity.
Why is this not seen? Consider the following four analogies.
The general illustration reveals that all is mind-only;

Each of the four metaphors possesses four contemplations:
first, that which is precisely "mind-only";
second, that because it is mind-only, it is empty.
Third, because it is mind-only, it is provisional; fourth,

this is the meaning of the Avataṃsaka Sūtra’s dream analogy.
The analogy of a reflection illustrates neither coming nor going;
the analogy of a shadow illustrates neither emerging nor entering;
the analogy of a magical illusion illustrates neither existence nor non-existence.
The analogy of an echo is neither conjoined nor dispersed;

Questioning the Forty-third Point of the Previous Treatise on Seeking Birth in the Pure Land:
It is asked, "The dharma of a bodhisattva should be to deliver sentient beings;
why then do they only go to the pure land of the Buddha Amitāyus?"
Answer: There are two kinds of bodhisattvas.
The first are those who possess abundant compassion and act for the sake of sentient beings.
The second are those who extensively accumulate the merits of all buddhas.
Those who delight in accumulating much merit shall reach the pure land of the One Vehicle, the Land of Immeasurable Life;

Contemplate the sixteen sublime realms of the Buddha’s primary and secondary environments;

They enter deeply into the five gates,

Whether with a distracted mind or a concentrated mind,

I set the completion of my life as my term.

It is like holding up a bright mirror and seeing one's own facial reflection,

It comforts and gladdens my heart,

They remain far removed from the works of Māra;

Seven days prior, he knew in advance that the time had arrived;
