Following behind the Buddha,
they will be reborn in that land in the time it takes to snap one's fingers.

complete with all the marks of excellence.
In the Forest of Radiant Jewels,
he expounded the sublime Dharma;
having heard it, [the king] immediately realized the patience regarding the non-arising of all phenomena (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).
Abiding in the stage of the right determination,
they never again regress,
ultimately reaching the state of being one birth away from Buddhahood.
The emanation body is sovereign,
pervading throughout the ten directions within immeasurable lands.
Having attained perfect enlightenment,
he sports and establishes his transformation through teachings in places of extreme suffering.
In every thought-moment,
they cause unspeakably unspeakable numbers of sentient beings to resolve upon Bodhicitta.
In every thought-moment...
May unspeakably unspeakable numbers of sentient beings be established in the conduct of Samantabhadra;
may their accumulations of merit and wisdom be fully perfected,
and may they together realize unexcelled, perfect enlightenment.
Each adorns a pure land and each gathers and transforms sentient beings,
just as our World-Honored One does.
They are equal and without distinction.
As long as all empty worlds exist, and as long as sentient beings,
karma, and afflictions persist, [so shall this remain].

I now invoke the name of Amitābha, The Buddha of True Merit;
I pray that you, out of compassion, will grant me your acceptance, Witnessing my repentance and my aspirations.
All the evil karma I have created in the past Arises entirely from beginningless greed, hatred, and delusion.
I now repent of everything produced by my body, speech, and mind; May I,
at the time when my life is about to end, Have all obstacles completely removed,
And behold that Buddha Amitābha face-to-face, Immediately attaining rebirth in the Land of Peace and Bliss.
The assembly of that Buddha was entirely pure; at that time, I was born from a supreme lotus and personally beheld the Tathāgata Amitābha.

The power of wisdom is vast and pervasive throughout the ten directions, universally benefiting the realms of all sentient beings.

Universal Exhortation for the Formation of the Lotus Society. Preface by Zhang Lun. Thus have I heard:
In the Western Quarter there is a Buddha named Amitābha.
One is named Immeasurable Light,
and one is named Immeasurable Life.
Furthermore, there are the two bodhisattvas Avalokiteśvara and Mahāsthāmaprāpta.
Assisting the Buddha to propagate his transformation,
they all, by the power of their great vows,
deliver and save all sentient beings.
That land is adorned with the seven treasures;
it is pure and spontaneous,
free from all impurities, and is therefore called a Pure Land.
Those people are all born through transformation from lotus flowers.
Their lifespans are immeasurable,
and they enjoy clothing, food, and other necessities.
They arrive according to their recollection;
furthermore, there are no sufferings,
nor is there any cyclic existence.
It is also called the World of Ultimate Bliss.
By looking back from this perspective at the body we currently possess and the world in which we dwell,
and comparing them to that land:
Regarding purity and defilement, lifespan, suffering and joy, birth and death—
how could the difference between them merely be that of heaven and earth?
Yet those who are ignorant do not realize this.
Some may know [the truth] yet lack faith;
they create their own obstacles,
clinging to perverted views with delusion.
They do not contemplate liberation;
abandoning this life, they are reborn there. How tragic this is!
Therefore, I now exhort all those with the karmic affinity to establish this Lotus Society,
even though it may be difficult to understand and difficult to discern.
One should still exert oneself with diligent effort;
how much more so since the name of the Buddha is so easy to uphold and the Pure Land is so easy to reach.
Among the eighty-four thousand Dharma gates,
there is no such shortcut;
one need only set aside a brief moment of leisure during the early morning.
Thus, it can serve as a resource that remains indestructible for eternal kalpas.
In this way, the effort expended is extremely slight,
yet the merit achieved is inexhaustible.
Why do sentient beings also suffer by abandoning themselves and failing to practice?
Alas! Dreams and illusions are not real;
longevity and early death are difficult to predict.
The interval of a single breath is itself the next life;
once one loses this human body, [it is gone forever].
Ten thousand kalpas will pass before there is recovery.
If one does not awaken at this moment,
what can the Buddha do for sentient beings?
I pray that you will deeply contemplate impermanence and not merely leave yourself with regret.
This was the exhortation for the occasion provided by the lay devotee Zhang Lun, who seeks purity and joy.

May it be that from this life onward,

They will not encounter false teachers,

and on the day their lives come to an end—
Free from illness and suffering,

Wandering through the realms of the ten directions,

*Praise for the Manifestation of the Pure Land Painted with Gold, Silver, and Clay* By Li Bai, Hanlin Academician. I have heard:

where the sun sets, lies a distance of ten trillion *kṣetras* from the Central Kingdom.
There is a world called Sukhāvatī.
The Buddha of that land has a body sixty million *koṭis* of *gaṅgā-nadī-vāluka* *yojanas* in height.
Between his eyebrows is a white tuft of hair (*ūrṇā-kośa*).
It turned clockwise,
like five Mount Sumerus;
its gaze was a bluish-white.
If the waters of the four great oceans were to sit upright and preach the Dharma,
they would remain serene and eternally present.
The ponds have clear golden sands;
precious trees line the banks,
and railings cover them completely.

and mother-of-pearl and lapis lazuli served as the ornaments for the towers and palaces.

all are realized by the Buddhas.
There is no falsehood here.

whether one has already made a vow or has not yet made a vow.

Jewel nets and precious jewel-trees, celestial flowers scattered upon fragrant pavilions—these painted images remain vividly before my eyes.

Adorned with five-colored [robes],

the golden body complete with the marks and signs, the spiral topknot, the white tuft between the brows, and the deep blue eyes.

To repay boundless kindness, one dedicates immeasurable blessings to the Western Pure Land. *Praise of the Western Pure Land*, by the Master Zhìyuán of Gūshān: "The principle of Heaven is profound and still."
How can one say it is pure or defiled?
Is it long or short? Is it that or this?
Yet those who engage in deliberation and conjecture fail to realize this;
however, once they awaken to it,
they become sages and become true.
It is for cultivating virtue, for attaining enlightenment,
for returning to the source, and for nirvana; yet,
if one is deluded by it, it becomes the state of an ordinary person and of delusion.
Is it the nature-virtue? Is it the union with sense-objects?
Is it following the current? Is it birth and death? How great it is!
The Sage is one who awakens first;
out of compassion for those who have not yet awakened,
he thus manifests the purity of the earth.
His lifespan shall extend for immeasurable eons;
he sits upright, facing east,
with eyes of compassion that look upon all without partiality.
Thus, may my fellow deluded ones grow weary of defilement and rejoice in purity;
loathing this Sahā world, may they take up residence in that Land of Peaceful Nurturing.
Thereafter, ascending to the jewel-adorned realm, they shall behold the Dharma King.
Through the divine transformations of the eye and the wondrous instruction of the ear,
the nature of profound stillness is restored without departing from it.
The vast emptiness of the ten directions is entirely manifested from my own mind;
how much more so the lands that depend upon that emptiness?
What else could there be?
Alas! Among those who have realized such awakening, who does not do so through revulsion toward impurity and delight in purity?
The urge toward evil and the desire for good arise from the mind that abandons the former and grasps the latter;
how much more so when one penetrates both joy and aversion to reach a state where there is neither joy nor aversion?
Is it not to know love and hate while being free from love and hate,
and to know acceptance and rejection while being free from acceptance and rejection?
For this reason, Śākyamuni manifested a defiled land in order to inspire weariness with it.
"Amitābha manifests his Pure Land to inspire joy—
how profound is its intent!
This was my compassionate mother, Lady Ma."
He felt revulsion toward the defiled realm of birth and rejoiced in the pure land of death;
he passed away at the age of seventy-one.
At the time when he was bedridden with illness,
he entrusted me with the worship and service of the Amitābha Buddha image of the Pure Land that he had created.
Ten years have passed since then.
Alas! The virtue of a mother extends no further than saving her child from drowning or falling into water and fire.
Furthermore, my mother was first able to renounce me for the sake of becoming a follower of the Buddha,
and subsequently was able to provide me with the means to study the Dharma.
Furthermore, Master, you have spoken of my rebirth in the Pure Land;
this is truly how you can instruct me in the Way. It brings to mind the lament of the "Liao-e" (The Sweet Flag and Mugwort) poem.
The sorrow of the wind-whipped tree;
though the years and months pass away,
my heart does not falter.

Thereupon, with solemnity and purity, he incensed the burner and dipped his brush to compose a hymn in praise of the Pure Land, praying that his mother might be blessed to ascend the steps of the sages.

1. The ocean of awakening is clear, perfect, vast, and boundless—neither constricted nor extended; yet this entire multitude, having lost their way, has for kalpas forfeited their family treasure amidst the surging tides of birth and death. 2. Having ascended the golden terrace, I behold the countenance of the Buddha and realize my own wondrous luminosity. 4. In the *Praise of Amitāyus Buddha* by the Great Wisdom Vinaya Master Yuanzhao: "The eighty-four thousand wondrous marks are none other than the Amitābha of one's own original nature."
The distant reaches of ten trillion lands are,
in truth, the Pure Land of the Mind-Only;
though purity and defilement may seem separated.
How could it transcend one's own mind?
Buddhas and sentient beings are merely distinct therein.
How could it ever deviate from one's own nature?
The substance of the mind is vast and empty,
unimpeded by coming and going;
its nature is fundamentally all-encompassing.
What prevents one from adopting or rejecting?
Therefore, by raising a single thought,
one immediately ascends to the realm of jewels.
Returning to my native land of Jambudvīpa,

truly, we have met as father and son in our original nature.
Those born of karmic conditions bear a debt of virtue,
yet they suffer in vain through the cycle of delusion;
today they cast themselves in sincere devotion.
I shall surely receive their salvation;
my threefold resolve is fully awakened,

To rely upon and uphold [this practice] until the end of time;
to praise it throughout dust-motes and lands.
A Praise for the Painting of Amitābha. By Su Shi (Wenzhong Gong), the husband of Lady Wang.

it is like a realm of a thousand *li*, traversed entirely within a single moment of dream.

I have heard that Emperor Ming of the Song dynasty once commissioned a golden image eighteen feet in height.
The four castings were unsuccessful;
thereupon, they were changed to fourteen *zhang*.
Yue then [consulted] Zhi Jing of Baima Temple.
He led those with common aspirations to transform an eighteen-foot statue of Amitābha Buddha in order to fulfill his vow;
he began by gathering gold and copper.
During the period of turmoil at the end of the Qi dynasty,
it was not until the beginning of the Liang dynasty that the matter was reported to the throne;
an imperial edict was subsequently issued granting permission.
Materials, officials, and artisans were provided as required.
On the third day of the fifth month in the eighth year of the Tianjian era, [the work was completed].
He commissioned the casting at Xiaozhuangyan Monastery;
when forty thousand *jin* of copper had been melted and poured for the body of the Buddha of Original Measure, it had not yet reached the chest.
The common people threw copper into the furnaces and smelting works,
yet as they cast it, the molds were never filled.
They reported this matter once again.
An imperial edict ordered three thousand jin of copper;
as the treasury was just beginning to measure it out for delivery,
word had already spread that the casting site was ready.
The imperial decree ordered that the bronze cauldrons be brought to the foundry;
they were subsequently melted down together,
and the casting was completed in a single smelting.
The people who had come were all left behind;
only when the bronze arrived at the terrace did they realize that their prior arrival was due to the power of spiritual inspiration.
When the mold was opened and measured,
it had surged to nineteen *zhang* in height,
yet its radiant features remained without deviation.
There were two large coins found among the strips of clothing;
their divine mystery was unfathomable.
When the initial clay image was completed,
Master Daozhao was performing prostrations and repentance rituals during the night.
Suddenly, he saw the image radiating a brilliant, vast light.
Three days after the casting was completed,
there was a monk named Daodu who assisted with the expenses to open the mold.
From afar, he saw two monks kneeling as they opened the topknot of the statue;
suddenly, they vanished.
When the statue was moved back to Guangzhai Temple, [the same occurred].
It had been a long time since rain was obtained,
and there was considerable dust and grime.
Suddenly, during the night, a light rain fell, moistening the ground.
When Master Sengyou was walking in meditation before the image,
he suddenly saw a flame of light above and below the image,
resembling a lamp or candle.
That night, the merchants on the Huai River all heard the sound of hundreds of people urging them to repair the bridge.
Since the Buddha-dharma flowed eastward, no miraculous manifestation of a golden image has surpassed this one.
Biography of Dharma Master Shenluan of Bigu Valley during the Later Wei Dynasty. Dharma Master Shenluan of Bigu Valley during the Later Wei Dynasty was Shi Tanyuan (Shi Tanluan), a native of Yanmen.
When he was young, he traveled to Mount Wutai;
moved by its spiritual wonders,
he vowed to leave the secular world.
He thoroughly mastered the principles and texts of the three vehicles, both sudden and gradual;
by nature, the Master was fond of esoteric arts and techniques.
Hearing that Tao Hongjing, the Hermit of Yinju in Jiangnan, possessed methods for attaining longevity,
he traveled a thousand li to seek him out.
Tao immediately bestowed upon him ten scrolls of the *Xianjing* (Scriptures on the Immortals) which he had studied.
The Master was filled with joy and self-assurance,
believing that the state of a divine immortal could certainly be attained.
Later, he returned to Luoyang.
He encountered the Tripiṭaka Master Bodhiruci and felt he had gained some understanding of his meaning;
he then questioned the Master, saying:
"Does the Buddha-way possess longevity?
Is it able to ward off aging and achieve immortality?
Zhi smiled and said:
"Longevity and immortality are the Way of our Buddha;
what place is there for them in the Daoist school?
He then bestowed the *Sutra of the Sixteen Contemplations* upon him, saying:
If you can recite this,
then there will be no further birth within the three realms,
and no eternal departure upon the ten paths.
As for longevity, there is nothing— whether fullness or emptiness,
waxing or waning, calamity or fortune, success or failure— that can reach it.
There are kalpa-stones and there are river sands;
while the number of sands and stones is finite,
the measure of his lifespan is infinite.
"This is the longevity of our Golden Immortal (the Buddha).
Upon hearing these words,
Luan conceived a profound faith.
He then burned the Daoist scriptures he had studied and devoted himself exclusively to contemplating the Buddhist sutras;
he cultivated the three meritorious deeds and visualized the nine lotuses.
Although he was beset by the changes of cold and heat and the invasions of illness,
he did not slacken in his initial resolve;
the Wei ruler took pity on his noble aspirations.
He was known as Shenluan.
One night, while he was engaged in his recitations,
a foreign monk suddenly entered the room with a dignified air and said:
"I am Nāgārjuna. That which I inhabit is the Pure Land.
Because you possess the aspiration for the Pure Land, I have come to see you."
The phoenix asked,
"How shall you instruct me?
The tree replied:
That which has already passed cannot be reached;
that which is yet to come cannot be pursued.
Where, then, does the present reside?
"The white colt is difficult to turn back.
Having finished speaking, he vanished.
Sengluan [recorded] these extraordinary events as he had witnessed them.
He knew for certain that the time of his death had arrived.
He immediately gathered the assembly and delivered an extensive discourse of instruction,
then commanded them to chant the name of Amitābha Buddha in a loud voice.
Luan then turned westward, closed his eyes, and passed away.
The entire assembly simultaneously heard the sounds of pipes, strings, and flutes coming from the west;
after a long while, they fell silent.
The Wei ruler was moved by this and ordered that he be buried west of the Fen River,
where a stele was erected to record his deeds and character.
The *Longshu Jingtuwen* states:
According to the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*, there are ten kinds of immortals (*ṛṣi*),
all of whom have a lifespan of ten million years.
When their merit is exhausted, they return to the cycle of saṃsāra,
because they have never fully realized the true nature;
thus they remain among the sentient beings of the six realms.
These seven realms share the same name;
they are all people within the cycle of saṃsāra. Among the people of the world, there are those who study the arts of the immortals.
Out of ten thousand, not one succeeds;
even if one were to succeed, they would still not escape saṃsāra,
for they remain attached to form and spirit and are unable to relinquish them.
Furthermore, form and spirit are merely delusive thoughts manifested within true nature;
they are not reality itself.
Thus, a poem by Hanshan says:
"Even if you were to become an immortal,
it would be no different from being a corpse-guarding ghost."
It is not like the Buddhist view of life and death, where one is as free as they please and unconstrained by anything.
Among those who have attained immortality since antiquity,
there have been none but Zhongli Quan and Lü Dongbin.
As for those who have studied under these two masters,
they surely number in the millions;
this is what I have personally heard from my own acquaintances.
Their number was not small;
in the end, they all died and were buried beneath the earth.
Indeed, one has spent one's life in vain,
exerting mental and physical effort to no avail. Yet,
one still desires to seek longevity.
Nothing compares to the Pure Land.
Those born in the Pure Land enjoy an immeasurable lifespan.
The greatness of attaining longevity is immense.
To study the arts of the immortals without cultivating this method is like discarding a magnificent jade gem that lies before one's very eyes.
Yet to seek after such an unattainable *yùfū* (a jade-like stone)—is this not delusion?

He never once displayed it to others for his own pride;

On the evening of his passing,

Biography of Dharma-Wisdom (Fazhi) Dharma Master of Tiantai during the Sui Dynasty. Regarding the biography of the Sui dynasty Tiantai Dharma-Wisdom Dharma Master:
Shi Fazhi traveled to study in Dongyue.

The World-Honored One Śākyamuni extended his broad and long tongue,

Single-mindedly recite the Buddha’s name.

On another day, he again experienced a vision in which the light from a celestial crown and jeweled vase shone upon his body.

The night was still far from dawn when Dayewang sat upon his meditation couch recollecting the Buddha;

Biography of Yu Xian, the Scholar of Upright Integrity of the Liang Dynasty. Yu Xian, courtesy name Yanbao, was a native of Xinye.
From his youth, he was remarkably intelligent;
there were none among the classics, histories, or the works of the hundred schools that he did not master.
As for his skill in chess and calculation,
he was peerless in his time; yet by nature,
he relied upon a state of equanimity and simplicity.
He was particularly fond of forests and springs;
of his ten-mu residence,

Subsisting on vegetarian food and wearing tattered clothes,

at one time, he traveled by boat.
Returning from Zhuzhong,
he loaded one hundred and fifty piculs of rice;
someone entrusted him with thirty piculs to carry.
When he arrived home, the person who had been entrusted with the grain said,

In his later years, he especially adhered to the teachings of Śākyamuni;

He performed prostrations and repentance during the six periods of the day and night, reciting the Lotus Sūtra once every day at its conclusion.

Emperor Wu heard of this and held him in high esteem.
He was posthumously titled the "Retired Scholar of Upright Integrity" (Zhenjie Chushi) to manifest his lofty and heroic character, as recorded in the *Nanshi*.

where the obscuring darkness is shattered and the nature of phenomena (dharmatā) is clearly revealed.
Having attained the fruit of true reality,
yet with ignorance not yet exhausted,
it moistens uncontaminated karma (*anāsrava-karma*).
Receiving the Dharma-nature Reward Body is called the Land of Fruitional Retribution;
this is because one contemplates the true reality (bhūtatathatā).
Because it is the fruit and retribution obtained by giving rise to true outflow-free wisdom (*anāsrava*), it is called "real.
Since the cultivation of its causes involves no fixed form or mind and is unimpeded,
it is also called the "Land of Real Retribution Without Obstruction."
The Avataṃsaka Sūtra clarifies that this is the world of Indra’s net.
As for the fourth, the Land of Constant Tranquil Light,
it is that which is illuminated by the ultimate wisdom of wondrous enlightenment.
The principle of suchness and the dharma-realm is called a "land," and it is also termed the "dharma-nature land."
However, true suchness and buddha-nature are neither body nor land, yet they are spoken of as body and land;
apart from the body, there is no land.
Apart from the land, there is no body.
As for what is called "land," it has two aspects:
first, the phenomenon; second, the principle.
The dwelling place of Vairocana as described in the *Samantabhadra-darśana-sūtra* is named the Constantly Quiescent Light (*nitya-prabhāsvara*).
It is asked: how does this relate to the ten kinds of Buddha-lands explained in the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra*?
Do these four encompass all [the perfections]?
Answer: How could they encompass only ten?
Furthermore, some people say:
The sūtra elucidates twenty-seven types of Buddha-lands;
the Land of Immeasurable Life is merely the sixth among them.
The present text addresses four [categories], encompassing them all without exception.
Question: Why does it not rely on ten or twenty-seven?
Answer: At first glance there is a textual basis;
however, because the intention is directed toward correlating [this] with the four teachings, it is difficult to discern.

The *Commentary on the Contemplation Sutra* clarifies the fundamental purport of the four lands (*catur-bhūmi*). This sutra takes the purification of the Buddha-land through the purity of mental contemplation as its fundamental purport.
There are four kinds of pure lands:
namely, the land where ordinary beings and sages dwell together,
and the land of residual existence through skillful means.
The Land of True Reward Without Obstruction is the Land of Constant Quiescence and Light. Each of these lands possesses its own degree of purity or defilement,
depending on the lightness or gravity of the five turbidities.
The coexistence of purity and impurity;
the analysis of essence versus function;
and the distinction between the pure and impure with remainder.
Entering progressively or instantaneously;
[realizing] the true recompense, the pure, or the impure;
[attaining] partial realization or ultimate perfection.
The tranquil light is pure and serene,
while the Sahā world is a mixture of evil;
it is filled with thorns and rubble.
The [Saha world] is filled with impurity;
it is defiled by cohabitation.
The Land of Peaceful Nurturing (An-yang) is pure.
The ponds flow with the eight virtues;
the trees are arrayed with the seven treasures; next is Nirvana.
All belong to the group of those with correct resolve;
ordinary beings and sages dwell together.
This is the Pure Land of the highest grade.
Regarding "having a remainder in terms of skillful means":
one cultivates the path of skillful means and abandons the delusions of the four abodes.
Therefore, it is called "expedient means" (*upāya*).
Because ignorance has not yet been exhausted, it is said to be "with remainder.
The *Śāstra* states:
Beyond the three realms lies a pure land,
wherein Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas are born;
there they receive the Dharma-nature body.
Within the non-sequential birth, there are further distinctions of sharp and dull faculties;
pointing upward is designated as pure,
while pointing downward is designated as defiled.
Regarding those who possess the unobstructed fruition of reality:
by practicing the Dharma of ultimate truth,
they realize a sublime retribution.
Because matter and mind do not obstruct one another, it is said to be "unobstructed.
It is inhabited solely by bodhisattvas, with no followers of the two vehicles (śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas).
As the *Benevolent Kings Sūtra* states:
The meaning is precisely this: "The three levels of worthies and the ten stages of sages abide in the retribution of their fruits.
This is the Flower Ornament Sutra’s "Infinite Cloud-Pavilions of Fragrance."
This refers to the pure and wondrous five sensory objects (*pañca-viṣaya*) of that land;
within these, one further discusses the distinctions of gradual and sudden enlightenment, as well as superior and inferior, purity and impurity.
As for the "Eternally Quiescent Light" (*nitya-prabhāsvara-ābhāsa*):
Constancy is the Dharma-body;
tranquility is liberation;
and radiance is prajñā.
These three dots are neither vertical nor horizontal, nor are they separate;
this is called the Secret Treasury (*guhyakośa*),
the dwelling place where all Buddhas and Tathāgatas roam and reside.
The ultimate, eternal, and supreme is the Pure Land;
it is merely that one attains varying degrees of ultimate purity or impurity according to whether one’s realization is superior or inferior.
Therefore, one should cultivate the wondrous contemplation of the mind.
The ability to attain the Pure Land constitutes the central tenet of this sutra.
The *Miaozong chao* (Commentary on the Essential Tenets) by Siming explains:
"The Dharma of the Mahāyāna..."
The essential point lies in the mind.
The attributes of the mind are easy to understand;
the attributes of form are difficult to comprehend.
Therefore, whether observing oneself or others,
one practices the contemplation of the mind;
now, one contemplates the Pure Land.
One must seek it within the mind,
for the mind is capable of encompassing all and the mind is capable of creating all.
"The mind is defiled, and the land is defiled;
the mind is pure, and the land is pure.
This is still a general indication.
This is not yet the definitive teaching.
The definitive point lies in the single mind,
where one suddenly cultivates the three contemplations.
This contemplation observes the environment and inhabitants of the Land of Peaceful Nurturing (An-yang);
because it is ultimately pure, it is called "purity of mental contemplation.
This contemplation is able to purify the four Buddha-lands.
In this way, such is the fundamental purport of this sutra. Regarding the initial point—
that those for whom the five turbidities are light constitute the "pure" realm of cohabitation—
this "purity" is extremely pervasive.
One must understand the distinct meaning.
For example, regarding the wholesome virtue of the precepts, this pertains to the stage of ordinary beings within the four teachings.
They are all able to cause the five turbidities to become light and thin,
thereby inducing a pure land of shared habitation;
thus, they perfectly contemplate lightness and turbidity.
The environment and its inhabitants are perceived as pure;
the primary and secondary worlds are supremely pure,
as stated in this sutra.

Having already observed each of the individual characteristics of the lands, this compares favorably with other sutras regarding the cultivation of various virtuous deeds to感召 (invoke) rebirth in the Land of Peaceful Nurturing (*Sukhāvatī*).
Its characteristics are exceptionally sublime; one should understand the four lands in detail according to the text, even unto where it says: "This sutra was originally intended for Vaidehī."
Disgusted with the defilement of the shared dwelling,
one seeks the purity of the shared dwelling;
therefore, the wondrous contemplation is expounded.
Contemplate their environment and its inhabitants;
if the three contemplations are perfected,
the coarse defilements will fall away first.
It is not that there is some other pure land; rather,
one must understand that the three contemplations are taught precisely for the purpose of being born in the Pure Land of Co-residence (sahā-vyūha).
This is truly because contemplating the subtle can destroy the three delusions;
it does not merely lead to rebirth in the Pure Land of Shared Residence.
According to the degree of shallowness or depth at which their afflictions are severed,
they naturally experience the three [nirvāṇas], such as that with remainder,
just as one who is ill requires medicine.
Originally seeking physical well-being,
he obtained an elixir recipe and prepared it for consumption.
Not only is the body at ease,
but it is also able to become light in its bones.
This physical ease may be likened to being born in the Pure Land of Shared Residence.
The "light bones" may be used as a metaphor for the response to the three higher lands;
they constitute a single medicinal efficacy.
Thus, it is profoundly superior that a single wondrous contemplation can purify all four lands.

The Collection on the Convergence of Myriad Virtues: An Elucidation of the Western Land. Sixfold Questions and Answers by Chan Master Yanshou Zhijue. Question: "The Pure Land of Mind-only pervades the ten directions."
How can one who has taken refuge in the lotus pedestal and entrusted their form to the Land of Peaceful Nourishment still harbor thoughts of acceptance and rejection?
Could such a person truly have reached the gate of non-arising?
If feelings of joy and aversion arise, how can there be equanimity?
Answer: For one who holds that the Buddha-land is solely mind, it arises only upon the full realization of the mind.
The *Tathāgatācintyaguhyanirdeśa-sūtra* states:
"All Buddhas of the three periods of time are entirely non-existent."
Relying solely on one's own mind,
if a bodhisattva can understand that all Buddhas and all phenomena are merely the measure of mind,
they will attain the patience of conformity (anulomikī-kṣānti).
Alternatively, one may enter the first bhūmi and,
upon casting off the body, be swiftly reborn in the Buddha-land of Sukhāvatī.
Therefore, know that it is only through the awakening of the mind that the Pure Land of Mind-only arises.
To be attached to objects is merely to fall into the realm of perceived objects.
Once it is clear that cause and effect do not differ,
one realizes that there are no phenomena external to the mind.
Furthermore, regarding the gate of equanimity and the principle of non-arising,
although one may look up to the teachings and give rise to faith,
how can one help but find that one’s strength is insufficient, one's contemplation shallow, and the mind restless as external objects are powerful and habitual tendencies are heavy?
One must be born in a Buddha-land to rely upon superior conditions; thus,
the power of patience will be easily perfected,
and one will swiftly traverse the bodhisattva path.
The *Śraddhotpāda Śāstra* states:
"When sentient beings first study this Dharma and seek to attain right faith..."
Their minds are timid and weak because,
while dwelling in the Sahā world,
they do not constantly encounter the Buddha.
Faith is difficult to achieve;
for those whose minds wish to retreat,
you should know that the Tathāgata possesses supreme skillful means.
To protect and sustain faith means that,
by means of the causal conditions of single-minded mindfulness of the Buddha,
one will be reborn in a buddha-field in accordance with one's vow.
One will constantly see the Buddha and be forever freed from the evil realms.
If a person single-mindedly contemplates Amitābha Buddha of the Western Quarter, [they shall attain rebirth].
They shall immediately attain rebirth there;
because they constantly behold the Buddha,
they shall never again fall back.
The *Wangsheng lun* (Treatise on Rebirth) states:
"Those who sport at the gates of hell are reborn in that land."
Having attained the patience of non-arising (anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti),
they return to the realm of birth and death to teach and transform those in the hells.
To rescue suffering sentient beings,
for this reason and by these causes and conditions,
one seeks rebirth in the Pure Land.
The *Ten Doubts Treatise* states:
"The Venerable Zhiyi ardently sought rebirth in the Pure Land,
yet he realized that the essence of birth is unattainable."
This is precisely true non-arising.
It is said that because the mind is pure, the Buddha-field is pure;
the deluded are bound by arising.
Upon hearing of "arising," they immediately form the understanding of arising; upon hearing of "non-arising," they immediately form the understanding of non-arising.
They do not know that arising is itself non-arising, and non-arising is itself arising.
Failing to comprehend this principle,
they recklessly engage in mutual criticism and contention;
such are people who harbor the wrong view of slandering the Dharma.
Question: Since one has practiced evil throughout a lifetime and accumulated deep causes, how can ten recitations at the moment of death suddenly dispel them?
Answer: The *Nāgasena-bhikṣu-sūtra* states:
The king asked the śramaṇa Nāgasena:
"If a person in this world commits evil for a hundred years..."
"I do not believe the words that one who recites the Buddha's name at the time of death will be reborn in a Buddha-land after passing away."
Nāgasena said:
"It is like placing a hundred large stones upon a ship;
because of the ship, they do not sink."
Although a person may possess inherent evil,
if they recite the Buddha's name for even a single moment,
they shall not enter the hells.
As for those small stones that sink,
they are like people who commit evil and do not know to recite the Buddha's name, thereby entering the hells.
Furthermore, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* asks:
Question: How can the mind for a brief moment at the time of death overcome the power of a lifetime’s conduct?
Answer: Although this mind lasts for only a short duration, [it is superior].
Yet the power of the mind is so fierce and sharp that it is like fire or poison;
though small, it can accomplish great things.
Because the mind at the time of death is resolute and courageous,
it surpasses the power of a hundred years of practice.
This subsequent mind is called the "Great Mind" because the functions of the faculties are urgent;
it is like a person entering battle who does not spare his own life, whom one calls brave.
Therefore, one knows that good and evil have no fixed nature;
their causal conditions are empty in essence.
Traces have their rises and falls;
affairs are distinguished by superiority and inferiority.
A single *liang* of pure gold—
It surpasses a hundred taels of layered silk;
like the faint glow of a torch,
it consumes the brushwood ten thousand fathoms high.
Question: Since there are no phenomena external to the mind and the Buddha neither comes nor goes, how can there be such things as seeing the Buddha or being welcomed by him?
Answer: It is through mindfulness of the Buddha that is solely of the mind.
By means of the contemplation of mind-only,
one universally encompasses all phenomena;
having realized that objects are nothing but mind, [one attains liberation].
When the mind is fully realized, it is itself the Buddha;
therefore, whatever one contemplates is none other than the Buddha.
As the *Pratyutpanna Samādhi Sūtra* states:
It is like a person who, in a dream, sees seven treasures and their kinsmen and rejoices;
upon waking, they remember them but do not know where they are.
Thus one recollects the Buddha.
This metaphor is a manifestation of mind-only;
it exists and yet is empty.
Therefore, there is neither coming nor going.
Furthermore, as an illusion is not real,
both mind and Buddha are equally absent.
Yet, as illusory appearances are not non-existent,
the Buddha of the mind is not destroyed; thus,
emptiness and existence are without obstruction.
Thus there is neither coming nor going,
yet it does not hinder universal seeing;
seeing is itself non-seeing.
Always in accord with the Middle Way,
the Buddha truly does not come,
and the mind likewise does not go.
When the path of resonance and response intersects,
one perceives only what the mind itself manifests—
just as sentient beings who have committed transgressions perceive the appearances of the hells.
The *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* states:
"Just as in all hells, beings collectively perceive hell-wardens and the like who are capable of inflicting harm."
Therefore, all these are manifestations of the minds of sinful beings due to their evil karma;
there are no actual copper dogs, iron snakes, or other such things existing externally to the mind.
This applies to all phenomena and things in the world.
It is likewise so;
for the land of Vairocana Buddha is not restricted to the east or the west.
If one attains correct understanding,
then both habitual tendencies and accumulated afflictions will be extinguished,
and both principle and cognition will be embraced.
He asked Layman Pang, "When speaking of the Buddha-land from the perspective of worldly affairs,
it is said to be one hundred thousand li away."
The great ocean is vast and boundless;
when stirred, black winds arise. Though those who have gone forth may number in the thousands or tens of thousands, [they are all swept away].
Among those who have attained realization, there are not even one or two.
Suddenly encountering the person of original nature,
they do not abide within the realm of causes and conditions.
How can one reconcile this and realize rebirth?
Answer: If we examine the fundamental tenet and investigate the source, it does not even speak of the existence of a Buddha or a land.
How could one say that what has been reached is not reached?
Therefore, the true nature is spontaneously possessed;
it does not involve causes and conditions.
Without moving so much as a hair’s breadth,
one constantly remains in profound stillness within the true essence.
If discussed in terms of phenomena:
Therefore, it is not a single level;
those of the nine grades of rebirth reach both the upper and lower realms.
Some may travel through lands of transformation and behold the Buddha’s response body;
some may be born in the land of retribution and perceive the Buddha’s true essence;
or some may ascend to the higher stages in a single night.
Some may realize the Lesser Vehicle only after the passage of an eon;
some possess sharp faculties while others possess dull faculties;
some have a concentrated mind while others have a distracted mind.
Whether awakening is swift or slow depends on the differing capacities of one's faculties;
whether the flower blooms early or late depends on the varying temporal limits.
These matters are fully recorded in both ancient and modern texts.
Ordinary beings and sages alike are born with it;
its mode of activity is clearly manifest,
and it is a vivid testimony confirmed by direct observation.
The Buddha’s Brahma-voice never deceives people.
As stated in the *Sukhāvatīvyūha Sūtra*:
The Buddhas of the ten directions, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges,
extend their broad and long tongues,
completely covering the great trichiliocosm.
To realize rebirth—how could this be empty talk?
It is asked: The Vimalakīrti Sūtra says:
Having accomplished eight qualities,
one will move through this world without blemish.
They are born in the Pure Land.
What are these eight? They are those who benefit sentient beings.
Yet they do not expect a reward;
on behalf of all sentient beings,
they undergo all manner of suffering and affliction.
All the merit they have performed,
they bestow entirely upon others,
maintaining a mind of equanimity toward all sentient beings.
Being humble and unimpeded,
they regard all bodhisattvas as if they were Buddhas.
Regarding sutras not previously heard,
one hears them without doubt and does not contradict them with the teachings of the śrāvakas.
One does not envy the offerings of others,
nor does one exalt one's own gains;
rather, within these circumstances, one subdues the mind.
Constantly examine one's own faults and do not speak of the shortcomings of others;
always seek all merits with a single-minded focus.
Question: How can those of inferior conduct and meager merit attain rebirth there?
Answer: In principle, one must be fully endowed [with the necessary conditions].
This belongs to the great root.
It is free from the eight defects and achieves the highest grade.
Just as among those of middle or inferior capacity,
one who possesses but a single dharma and whose resolve is firm and unshakable [will attain the goal].
One may also attain the lower grade.
Question: The Contemplation Sūtra elucidates the sixteen gates of contemplation;
all of these involve concentrating the mind to cultivate meditative concentration.
By contemplating the Buddha’s marks and signs until they are clearly understood as perfectly luminous,
one finally ascends to the pure realm.
How can one who is in a state of distracted mind perform transformation and travel?
Answer: The nine grades of the sūtra text naturally possess degrees of elevation and descent;
though they encompass both the upper and lower levels, they do not transcend these two states of mind.
First, those who stabilize their minds by practicing meditative concentration and cultivating contemplation attain rebirth in the highest grade.
Second, those who single-mindedly recite only the Name [of the Buddha] attain rebirth in the middle grade.
Sustained by the permeation of various virtues,
one dedicates them and makes vows,
thereby attaining the lower grade.
One must still take refuge for the duration of one's life,
practicing with diligent cultivation until the end of one's term,
whether sitting or reclining.
Always face westward.
While performing prostrations during the practice of the Way,
and at the time of reciting the Buddha's name and making vows:
With earnest and sincere devotion,
free from all other thoughts,
as if facing execution.
Whether one is in prison,
pursued by vengeful enemies,
or beset by water or fire.
With single-minded resolve, I seek salvation;
may I be delivered from the burden of suffering and swiftly realize non-arising.
To extensively deliver all sentient beings,
to perpetuate and honor the Triple Gem,
and to vow to repay the four debts of gratitude.
Such sincere resolve shall certainly not be in vain; however,
should one's words and deeds fail to correspond, [the merit will be lost].
The power of faith is feeble;
there is no mind of continuous succession from moment to moment,
but rather a disposition characterized by frequent interruptions.
Relying on such indolence,
one hopes for rebirth at the time of death;
however, one will be obstructed solely by karmic hindrances.
It is feared that it will be difficult to encounter a virtuous friend;
oppressed by wind and fire,
right mindfulness will not be established.
Why is this? The present moment is the cause and the time of death is the effect;
therefore, the cause must be real.
Thus, the fruit is not in vain;
for when the sound is harmonious, the resonance follows suit,
and when the form is straight, the shadow is upright.
If one wishes to achieve the fulfillment of the ten recitations at the time of death,
one should simply prepare the ferry and the bridge in advance by accumulating and combining meritorious virtues.
If, at the time of dedication,
one's every thought remains undiminished,
then there will be no cause for anxiety.
Now, the two wheels of good and evil and the two retributions of suffering and pleasure are all created by the three karmas and produced by the four conditions.
Produced by the six causes and subsumed within the five fruits,
even a single moment of mind characterized by anger or sexual misconduct [yields these results].
That which is the karma of hell is stinginess, greed, and unreality;
that which is the karma of hungry ghosts is likewise.
The darkness of ignorance and delusion is the karma of animals;
arrogance and haughtiness are the karma of asuras.
The cultivation of asura-karma;
the firm observance of the five precepts is human-karma.
Diligently cultivating the ten wholesome actions is the karma of the heavens;
it leads to the realization of the emptiness of persons.
To know that the nature of conditions is detached is the practice of the śrāvaka. To know that conditions themselves are detached is the practice of the pratyekabuddha.
The simultaneous cultivation of the six perfections is the activity of a bodhisattva;
it is true compassion, impartial and equal.
This is precisely the work of the Buddha.
If the mind is pure, one is born through transformation in a pure land of fragrant terraces and jeweled trees;
if the mind is defiled, one receives a physical form in a foul land of hills, mounds, pits, and ravines.
These are all fruits of equal status that can evoke superior conditions; therefore,
they are removed from the source of one's own mind.
There is no separate essence.
As the Vimalakīrti Sūtra says:
"If one wishes to attain a pure land..."
One need only purify one's own mind;
as the mind is purified,
so too is the Buddha-field purified.
Furthermore, a sutra says:
"Because the mind is defiled, sentient beings are defiled;
because the mind is pure, sentient beings are pure."
The Avataṃsaka Sūtra says:
"For example, like the precious heart-king jewel,
sentient beings see it according to their own minds."
Because the minds of sentient beings are pure,
they are able to see pure lands.
The *Mahāsannipāta Sūtra* says:
If you wish to purify your realm,
simply purify your own mind;
thus it should be known.
All things return to the mind;
the myriad dharmas arise from me.
If you wish to attain the pure fruit, [you must cultivate this].
One should simply practice pure causes;
just as the nature of water is to flow downward and the nature of fire is to rise upward,
such is the force and sequence of things.
What cause for doubt is there?

*The General Praise of Amitābha: Revealing the Essential Meaning of the Western Land*. Questioned by the Dharma Master Kuiji of Ci'en: "The bliss of the Buddha-lands in the ten directions is all the same."
Why is it that [the Buddha] universally points toward the West and exhorts people to be born there?
The answer is: it is precisely because ordinary beings have heavy karma and give rise to craving everywhere.
If one does not direct the gaze toward a single direction,
the mind will not be bound in focused concentration.
Therefore, the Lotus Sūtra says:
Sentient beings are attached everywhere;
he leads them so that they may emerge from it.
Furthermore, the Pure Land of the West is supreme.
I pray that you will strongly and universally exhort [beings] to be reborn there so that they may swiftly attain the fruits of sainthood;
this is why I point to it everywhere.
Question: The celestial palace of Maitreya is no small place of happiness, and there are many excellent companions there.
Why is it necessary to earnestly exhort one to be reborn in the Western Paradise?
Answer: If one discusses Tuṣita,
it surpasses the human realm and is even equal to the Western [Pure Land].
Since all accomplishments are extremely inferior,
he exhorts one to be born in the Western Land,
so as to abandon the inferior and seek the superior.
Regarding superiority and inferiority:
the Pure Land is superior in ten ways, while the celestial palaces of the gods are inferior in ten ways.
As for the ten ways in which the Pure Land is superior:
First, the excellence of the abode of the transformer;
second, the excellence of the longevity of those to be transformed;
third, the excellence of the realm being non-bound to a specific world-system.
Fourth is the excellence of purity and freedom from desire in all directions;
fifth is the excellence of not dwelling among women;
sixth is the excellence of non-retrogression in spiritual practice.
Seventh is the excellence of the seven purities being free from defilement;
eighth is the excellence of the adornment of the buddha-field;
ninth is the excellence of mindfulness of the Buddha in gathering the faculties.
Regarding the ten points where rebirth through ten recitations is superior and the celestial palaces are inferior:
first, the land inhabited is inferior.
Second, the lifespan of those being converted is short and inferior;
third, their inclusion within the three realms of existence is inferior;
fourth, those gods possess the inferiority of desire.
Fifth, the inferiority of mixed residence for men and women;
sixth, the inferiority of regression in spiritual practice;
seventh, the inferiority of impure regions rather than pure ones.
8. Inferiority in the adornment of the eight lands;
9. Inferiority in the mastery of the emotions through virtuous mindfulness;
10. Inferiority in the toil and hardship of spiritual practice.
There are these ten excellences and ten deficiencies;
for this reason, one is exhorted to be born in that Land of Bliss.
It is asked: why is it that the sentient beings in that land have no manifold sufferings?
[Question: They only experience various pleasures;
how is it that they have no manifold sufferings?
[Answer: It is because the sentient beings of that land...
Born through transformation from a lotus, there is no suffering of birth;
the four seasons cannot cause change, so there is no suffering of death;
not being a body subject to fragmentation, there is no suffering of illness.
Their lifespan is inexhaustible and free from the suffering of death;
they have no parents, nor distinctions between kin and strangers;
and they are free from the suffering of encountering those one hates.
Their desires are fulfilled according to their wishes;
they suffer no pain of not obtaining what they seek,
and their countenances are upright and majestic.
They are free from the suffering of impaired or deformed sense faculties;
throughout the four seasons they remain uniform,
free from the suffering of cold or heat.
In this Sahā world, the impure physical body is constrained by four serpents and its life is threatened by three dragons.
Deviating from the norm brings illness and affliction;
when karma is exhausted, death invades.
Where there is attachment, separation is inevitable.
Without resentment, there is no meeting;
for one is deluded regarding the ultimate truth and thus recklessly ensnared by the aggregates.
Now, for those whom [the Buddha] universally loves,
such things as these exist forever no more;
therefore, it is said that "there are no manifold sufferings."
Is it not that one will not only soon escape coarse suffering, but also that the sublime fruit is not far off? Question:
If one performs wholesome deeds at the time of death, one immediately attains rebirth in the Pure Land.
"Why need one beforehand cultivate various superior karmas?
Answer: "The length of human life—whether it be long or short—is difficult to fathom;
one may suddenly fall ill, become exhausted, and lose consciousness."
Or they may suddenly pass away before their time;
since this concerns the merits accumulated during one's life,
it is difficult to escape the calamities of the next world.
One should cultivate virtuous conditions in advance, fearing and guarding against such faults.
Question: Regarding the ten recitations of Amitābha that lead to immediate rebirth in the Pure Land.
According to what has been stated here, the fruit is manifest while the cause is subtle. Why, then,
does the *Sukhāvatīvyūha Sūtra* declare that one cannot be born in that land through small roots of goodness, merit, or causal conditions?
Answer: Rebirth is attained through ten recitations.
To guide those sentient beings who are indolent, [the Buddha] subsequently speaks of many virtuous causes and conditions.
This is intended for those who practice with diligence;
whether extensive or concise,
the principles do not contradict one another.
Question: Does the person who attains rebirth possess an intermediate state body (*antarābhava*)?
Answer: Regarding this, the *Qunyi lun* (Treatise on Resolving Doubts) presents two views.
The first states that those of extreme goodness or extreme evil do not possess an intermediate state body.
Second, it is said that there is no distinction between good and evil;
as long as there is the relinquishing of a previous existence and the undergoing of a new birth, an intermediate state (antarābhava) exists in all cases.
Because it serves as the vehicle for the transmission of consciousness,
there would be no intermediate state (antarābhava) except for those who manifest transformation-bodies in the present life.
Now, taking that which exists [in all cases] as the correct view.
*Jizhao ji Jian xifang yaoyi* (The Collection of Quiescent Illumination: An Examination of Essential Points Concerning the Western Region). It is unknown which master composed this text.

Yet, the *General Praise of Amitābha* does not mention the ten excellences of the Pure Land;

Each demonstrated skillful means.

Those who are masters of universal principles know where to turn according to their aspirations;

Answer: The gods of the desire realm are addicted to exquisite pleasures and intoxicated by the wine of sensual desire;

A Letter Requesting Dharma Master Siming to Remain in the World. This letter, addressed to Dharma Master Siming, was written by Yang Yi, Duke Wen. Your servant, Yang Yi, respectfully submits this: Recently...
I have humbly considered that the Great Master has resolved to form a monastic society with ten monks and pledged to enter into a three-year period of repentance.
Nevertheless, by entering the meditative absorption of the "flame-entrance," one resolutely attains rebirth in the Pure Land,
where the view of a self is instantly emptied.
The power of their vows becomes even more robust;
they ascend to the supreme rank of the Lotus and hear the ultimate sound of the Dharma-tree.
This matter is not empty;
it is what the former Buddhas have realized.
Nevertheless, within worldly thoughts, one earnestly maintains the heart of aspiration.
Truly, the Great Master thoroughly penetrated the ultimate aim of the three contemplations;
he was revered and admired by the fourfold assembly,
and he continued the life-force of wisdom of the Tiantai school.
He opened the gateway to the ultimate limits of transcendence;
through the ten wholesome acts, he guided people,
so that they vied with one another to preserve pure karma.
With a single voice supporting the teachings,
he extensively expounds the golden words;
his compassionate shelter is universally impartial.
The fragrance of the Way is truly harmonious;
it is the realm of Ultimate Bliss,
which is indeed the manifestation of the Buddha’s skillful means.
Yet this body of great suffering is not what the wise delight in;
were one to harbor preferences for or aversion toward it, [one would fail].
Thereupon, love and hatred arise;
once the mind of grasping and rejecting has sprouted,
the dualistic view of subject and object is born.
Truly, you possess profound insight and have long investigated the eternal truth;
yet you have condescended to accommodate those at the initial stage of practice.
I hope that strategic counsel may arise from pure conduct;
I humbly pray that, by virtue of receiving this gracious edict,
you may further expand the field of merit.
May the period of his life be extended,
may the prosperity of his transformative conditions be fully realized,
and may it be hoped that the time for this repentance ceremony will soon come to an end.
I have briefly followed the winding path of the Dharma to accompany you,
hoping to emulate Cunda by respectfully offering this final tribute.
I pray that you share in this joy,
so that we may suddenly cast off our worldly minds; I am fortunate to have moved your compassion for those who are ignorant and deluded.
Before you have yet entered into nirvana,
I earnestly hope that you will deign to listen;
I look forward with bated breath to your reply.
Respectfully submitted for your information.

A Letter in Reply to Master Yang Wengong Requesting that He Remain in This World. By the Dharma Master Zhili of Siming. Zhili respectfully writes this during an interval between his lectures and repentance rituals.

In this way, doubt does not arise in every thought-moment;
with every sound, one attains liberation,
joyfully encountering the wondrous reality.
May we vow to form superior causes and gather the provisions for enlightenment, widely inviting both the ordained and the laity,
so that the path-seeking mind may arise within the great assembly.
The auspicious assembly of ten years has fortunately been completed;
both within and without, all rejoice.
We respectfully extend this celebration and repentance.
I humbly reflect that Amitābha, the Compassionate Father, and Śākyamuni, the Guiding Teacher,
through their respective methods of severing and gathering,
together bring sentient beings to maturity according to their karmic conditions.
Without factionalism or partiality,
we shall together accomplish this superior enterprise;
it is my hope that the sentiments of those far and near will be fully realized.
With the forgetting of views regarding purity and defilement,
one shall not wait for Maitreya’s descent to be born,
but will swiftly realize the supreme grade of the Land of Quiescent Light.

Five Verses Encouraging the Practice of Buddha-Recitation by Chan Master Huishen of Cishou I. The Merit of Reciting the Buddha’s Name If one recites the name of Amitābha with a single thought, One shall surely attain rebirth in the Land of Ultimate Bliss. Even those who have committed the five grave offenses and ten evil deeds, Shall not fall into the three miserable realms. II. The Difficulty of Obtaining the Human Body To obtain a human body is as difficult as finding an udumbara flower; To encounter the appearance of a Buddha in the world is even more rare. If you do not practice while you still have this precious opportunity, When will you ever again find such a favorable time? III. The Suffering of Birth and Death Birth and death are like a wheel turning incessantly; The cycle of existence is as vast as the great ocean. From beginningless time until now, we have wandered through it all; How can we find peace and rest within this endless flow? IV. The Efficacy of the Buddha’s Vow The Vow of the Buddha of Infinite Life is most profound and wondrous; It can deliver beings from the sea of suffering and lead them to liberation. If you rely upon his power with a sincere heart, You will certainly be born in the Western Paradise. V. The Exhortation to Practice Now The Dharma-ending age is here; the path is perilous and steep. Do not wait for old age or sickness before you begin to seek the Way. Quickly take up the practice of Buddha-recitation; Only then will you avoid falling into the abyss of the three evil paths.

Three Verses on the Encouragement of Nianfo (Buddha-Recitation) for Transformation and Guidance By Vinaya Master Qingzhao Huiheng I. The Buddha’s Dharma is vast and profound, Yet its essence lies in the single word "Nianfo. To recite the Buddha’s name with focused mind Is to enter the gate of the Tathāgata’s wisdom. II. Sentient beings are drowning in the sea of suffering; Only by relying on the Buddha can they find safety. If you wish to escape birth and death, You must constantly practice the recitation of the Buddha’s name. III. The merit of Nianfo is boundless; It surpasses all other forms of giving and virtue. Even if one were to fill the world with jewels And offer them to the Buddhas of the ten directions, This would not equal a single moment of sincere recitation. Therefore, you should diligently cultivate this practice.

Renpiao, Huanzhu, Composed in Response to Yuanming’s “Return to the Plow,” for Lushi Zhu’an I have long harbored a desire to return to my mountain home, Yet I have been detained by the affairs of the world. Now that I have retired from official service, I am free to follow my heart’s true intent; I shall not let the years pass in vain. My fields and gardens are already prepared for cultivation, And my house and its surroundings are peaceful and tranquil. The birds sing out as they fly back to their nests, And the deer call to one another as they roam. The flowers bloom in profusion, And the trees are lush with greenery. The clear stream flows along its course, And the clouds drift across the sky. I shall enjoy myself in this place, Wandering freely among the hills and streams. I shall drink from the spring and pluck the herbs, And gather wild fruits to eat. I shall wander through the deep woods, And listen to the sounds of the valley. I shall gaze at the mountains and rivers, And contemplate the Way of Heaven. I shall not seek fame or profit, Nor pursue worldly honors. I shall simply live in accordance with nature, Content with what comes to me. This is my true intention, To return to the simplicity of my former life. May I never again be entangled in the dust of the world, But remain forever in this pure retreat. Thus, I bid farewell to all worldly ties, And return to the source of my being. This is my "Return to the Plow. May it be so.
