one forever casts off the baseness of the womb-prison.
His eyes opened and his tongue became fixed as proof was established;
the bull’s charge and the rooster’s pecking suddenly ceased;
and while standing within the Iron City, he defied the king’s decree.
One must maintain a sincere heart;
sitting upon the lotus throne, one relies on the Buddha’s grace and finds it difficult to cast aside the ultimate truth.
Should one happen to slander the Triple Gem or violate the precepts of discipline,
then at the moment when the winds and knives force the dissolution of the body, [the consequences will follow].
When the karma-mirror reflects one's form,
one encounters a spiritual friend who manifests inconceivable wonders:
the forest of swords transforms into seven rows of flowering trees.
The fiery chariots are transformed into lotus ponds of the eight virtues;
the hells subside, and as all things become serene, the mind of fear is entirely extinguished.
Celestial flowers flew and led the way;
in an instant, the Transformation Buddha welcomed him.
His eye of wisdom was clear and his mind was enlightened.
The incense burner fell from his hand;
it fulfilled the prophecy, yet the lotus did not wither.
He received the prediction of enlightenment, and before long, he reached the Jewel Forest (Ratnavana).
How marvelous!
The power of the Buddha is inconceivable, unprecedented in all time past or present.
The Chan Master has set his sole resolve upon the Western Paradise.
His words of praise were as grand as this;
even regarding the convergence of all virtues,
he earnestly exhorted others to cultivate and practice them.
Thus we know that the man of comprehensive understanding is without parsimony;
his kindness and benefit extend in manifold ways.
Compared to this, those who stagnate in stillness or sink into emptiness are far removed.
This *Fu* (rhapsody) has its own commentary by the Master himself;
the matters therein are extensive and the prose is lengthy.
It is not possible to record this all here.
A cursory examination of what pertains to it reveals that these are all the wondrous words of the sūtras.
As for the miraculous traces recorded in the *Wangsheng zhuan* (Biographies of Rebirth),
only those who are deeply learned in antiquity and devoted to the Way will,
upon beholding this essential outline, [appreciate its significance].
I have now fully understood the outline and details.

*An-yang Fu* (Rhapsody on the Peaceful Nurturing), Submitted in Accordance with Imperial Decree. *An-yang Fu*, Submitted in Accordance with Imperial Decree by Qian Chu, King of Wuyue. I have received and fully understood the imperial decree.
I have heard that in the Land of Peaceful Nurturing, the Pure Land of Amitābha,
all transformations come to rest.
If for a single thought one is not deluded,
one entrusts oneself to that holy embryo;
it will be as easy to return [to the source] as turning over one's palm.
Both faith and non-faith are equally suchness;
I tread upon this broad and level highway.
He was serene and lucid.
The Master led the fourfold assembly and established the principles of the One Vehicle.
You encourage me with the causes of the white moon and assist me with the fruits of the blue lotus;
you are a virtuous friend to humans and devas.
If not you, who else could it be?
My heart is filled with shame and gratitude;
this feeling remains with me morning and night.
Therefore, I hereby issue this encouragement and exhortation.
It is hoped that you will take full note of it.
This letter is sent with few further words.
Inscription on the Sun-Contemplation, with Preface. By Zunshi, the Patriarch of Repentance at Ciyun Monastery.
In the fourth year of the Tianxi era, the year of Gengshen, on the first day of the second month in spring, the *kǒuwèi* day.
On the thirteenth day, the sixteenth of the month (Jiwei),
at the side of Xianglin Cave on the eastern ridge of the mountain,
south of the Flying Peak of Mount Gṛdhrakūṭa, the Song dynasty śramaṇa Zunshe [established] the Ancient Indian Temple.
When the Riziguan Hermitage was completed, he inscribed a stone with the "Inscription on Riziguan," excerpted from the *Sukhāvatīvyūha-sūtra* (Sixteen Contemplations Sutra):
"Deeply follows that radiant spirit; The heart inclines like a sunflower; A remnant of the light from the Mōngfù [sunrise] shore."
The six dragons cease their movement; like a drum suspended from above, like the brilliance of a wall, they close their eyes and form a pair.
Through the accumulation of thoughts, the Lord is accomplished; the majestic circular image arises from within the hazy and indistinct.
Treading upon frost, one realizes its hardness will reach its limit; this depends upon manifest clarity.
Directing my thoughts toward the quarters, the deity of the precepts marches afar;
the chamber is here, therefore I face the long-streaked moon. A Verse for Painting an Image of Amitābha Buddha, with Preface. By the Layman Dongpo Shi and the Vinaya Master Yuanzhao of Qiantang.
He universally exhorted both monastics and laypeople to take refuge with sincere devotion in the Western World of Ultimate Bliss. —
Su Shi of Mei Mountain.
With reverence, she donated the hairpins, earrings, and other personal effects left behind by her deceased mother, Lady Cheng of Shu Commandery,
and commissioned the artisan Hu Xi to paint an image of Amitābha Buddha.
To dedicate merit for the peace of the deceased,
he spoke in verse: The Buddha,
with his great perfect enlightenment, Pervades and fills the realms of the ten directions.
Due to my inverted perceptions, I have drifted in and out of birth and death;
how can I, with a single thought-moment, attain rebirth in the Pure Land?
I have created karma since beginningless time, yet in a single thought-moment, there is already more than enough.
Having arisen from a single thought, it likewise ceases within that single thought.
At the place where arising and ceasing are utterly extinguished, I and the Buddha are one and the same—
like water cast into the sea, or like bellows blown by the wind.
Though there be great sages with wisdom, they too cannot discern it;
may my former parents and all sentient beings have the Western Land as their dwelling place, and may all they encounter be the realm of Ultimate Bliss.
Every person attains immeasurable life, Neither going nor coming.

Furthermore, he emits a light named "Beholding the Buddha"; This light awakens those whose end is near, Causing them to awaken to mindfulness and behold the Tathāgata, So that at the end of life they may be born in that Pure Land.
Seeing those at the point of death who are exhorted to recite the Buddha’s name, and being shown sacred images so that they may gaze upon them with reverence,
thereby causing them to develop deep faith and devotion toward the Buddha— this is why this light is attained.
These two verses [are as follows].
The first four lines praise the Buddha’s emission of light.
This light is named "Beholding the Buddha," for it enables those approaching the end of life to behold the Buddha and attain rebirth.
The final four lines praise the Buddha for cultivating the causes of this radiance.
These causes consist solely of exhorting those at the point of death to practice mindfulness of the Buddha (*buddhānusmṛti*) and showing them the image of the Buddha.
This radiance was attained at the time of his attainment of Buddhahood;
that he now extensively bestows these verses is intended to exhort those of deep faith.
Whenever one encounters a kinsman or any other person at the time of their death,
first place an image of the Buddha before the bed so that they may see it with their own eyes.
And one should encourage them to practice mindfulness of the Buddha. If they are oppressed by suffering,
or if they previously lacked faith and were unwilling to practice mindfulness of the Buddha, [one should still urge them].
Furthermore, one must employ various skillful means to encourage them to invoke the Buddha's name,
even down to ten recitations,
so that they may attain the extinction of grave offenses.
To be born in the Buddha’s Pure Land—
this single benefit is inconceivable.
If one can exhort even a single person to be born in the Pure Land, [the merit is immeasurable].
Even if one does not personally practice cultivation oneself,
one would still be entitled to birth in a Buddha-land;
how much more so when one will attain Buddhahood in the future.
They are able to emit radiance that illuminates all sentient beings;
at the moment of death, they behold the Buddha.
I have often seen people of this world who,
for the sake of affection and love,
gather their heads together and weep.
They do not think to rescue or deliver them.
How bitter, how bitter!
Such are called evil associates (pāpa-mitra).
Drawn by the bonds of affection,
one falls into the evil realms,
with no prospect of liberation.
There are five kinds of people in the world who are unwilling to practice mindfulness of the Buddha.
The first are those who previously lacked faith.
Second, attachment to wealth and treasures;
third, inability to renounce wife and children;
fourth, cherishing one's own body and life.
Fifth, being obstructed by sinful karma,
one falls into hell after death;
may you awaken to this quickly.
The Verse on Establishing Right Faith in Rebirth Based on the Sūtras is the same as before: "If there are those who can recite and uphold this verse..."
One obtains three kinds of benefits:
first, one is able to constantly uphold the titles of all Mahāyāna sūtras;
second, one is able to increase one's faith in the Pure Land.
Third, cause those who hear it to have deep faith in the Pure Land.
If one encounters someone who is approaching the end of life, chant [the name] aloud once or twice,
and then exhort them to recite the Buddha's name.
I prostrate to Amitābha, the World-Honored One of Great Compassion, in the Western Land of Peace and Bliss;
Relying upon various sūtras, I have accomplished the resolute faith in rebirth;
For those who abide in the Mahāyāna with a pure mind, ten recitations shall bring them to mind that Amitāyus.
"Dreaming of the Buddha at the moment of death ensures rebirth in the Pure Land"— thus it is said in the *Mahāratnakūṭa Sūtra*.
"When the fires of the hells of the five heinous crimes appear, if one encounters a virtuous friend and arouses a fierce resolve,
reciting the Buddha’s name ten times will lead to immediate rebirth"— thus it is said in the *Sukhāvatīvyūha Sūtra (Sixteen Contemplations)*.
If one possesses a heart of joy, faith, and delight, Even ten recitations will lead to rebirth there.
Were it otherwise, Buddhahood would not be attained; Thus it is stated in the Forty-Eight Vows.
All who hear the Name and give rise to a sincere mind, A single thought of dedication shall lead to rebirth there.
"Except for those who have committed the five heinous crimes or slandered the true Dharma— thus it is said in the *Sukhāvatīvyūha Sūtra*—
if at the time of death one is unable to contemplate or recollect [the Buddha], yet merely gives rise to the thought that the Buddha exists,
this person’s breath shall cease and they will be reborn there. Thus it is said in the *Mahābherīhāraka Sūtra*.
For one day and one night, suspend silk canopies; With single-minded devotion, let the thought of rebirth be uninterrupted.
While lying down, you will dream of the Buddha and attain rebirth; Thus it is said in the *Sukhāvatīvyūha Sūtra*.
Throughout the day and night, recite the Buddha’s name, Diligently and with earnest effort, without ceasing.
Exhorting one another in turn to be reborn together— Thus it is said in the *Mahākaruṇā-sūtra*:

"Whether for one day, two days, or seven days, if one holds fast to the Name with an undistracted mind, the Buddha will appear before them and they shall be reborn. Thus it is said in the *Sukhāvatīvyūha-sūtra*.

If a person hears of that Amitābha for one day, two days, or even longer, and maintains focused mindfulness before them, they will immediately attain rebirth there. Thus it is said in the *Pratyutpanna Samādhi Sūtra*:
"For ten days and ten nights, during the six periods of the day and night, prostrate with the five limbs to the Buddha and maintain uninterrupted mindfulness."
One sees that very Buddha in this very life and attains rebirth there; thus it is said in the Drum-Sound King Sūtra (*Dharmarāja-saṃghāṭa-sūtra*).

By observing the fast and precepts for ten days and ten nights, suspending silk banners and canopies, burning incense and lamps, and maintaining constant mindfulness without interruption, one attains rebirth there; thus it is said in the *Sukhāvatīvyūha-sūtra*.

If a person single-mindedly recollects a Buddha of one direction, whether walking or sitting, within seven weeks they will manifest before that Buddha and attain rebirth there; thus it is said in the Mahāsaṃnipāta Sūtra.
If a person vows to constantly practice walking meditation for ninety days, without sitting or lying down.
Within samādhi one beholds Amitābha; thus it is said in the *Sūtra on the Buddha Standing*.

If a person sits upright facing due west and constantly recollects the Buddha for ninety days, they will be able to achieve samādhi and be born before the Buddha; thus it is said in the *Mañjuśrī-prajñā Sūtra*.
I have spoken thus from but a small portion of the verses in the various sūtras; what has been said here is inexhaustible.
May those who hear it together give rise to right faith, for the Buddha’s words are true and free from deception.
To those who doubt, he says:
Contemplating this verse,
those who give rise to faith and joy for even a single thought-moment among the ten recollections—
even those who merely form the intention of knowing that the Buddha exists— [attain the same merit].
They will also be born in that land;
furthermore, there are those who attain birth only after seven times seven days, up to ninety days,
through the practice of mindfulness of the Buddha.
Is it not the case that the Pure Land is one and the same?
For what reason, then, do the cultivated causes differ so abruptly?
The explanation states:
Although the Pure Land is one,
those who are born there differ from one another;
the *Sukhāvatīvyūha Sūtra* categorizes them generally into three grades.
The *Sutra of the Sixteen Contemplations* opens this up into nine grades;
if it were further subdivided,
they would likewise be immeasurable.
Furthermore, a doubt arises:
since those of the lower grades have cultivated the causes only shallowly,
they ought to experience regression and fall.
The commentary states: This is not so.
It is merely that the blossoming of the nine grades of flowers has varying degrees of speed, and their distance from the Buddha varies.
Among those who have attained the Way, there are those of sharp and dull faculties; yet all who are born there are,
by rule, non-retrogressive.
The Sūtra says:
"All those who are born therein abide in the assembly of those destined for right certainty."
Furthermore, it says:
"All sentient beings who are born are all *avaivartika*."
This refers to non-retrogression.
In the *Ten Doubts Treatise*,
it is stated that there are five kinds of causes and conditions by which one does not retrogress.
First, because they are sustained by the power of Amitābha Buddha’s great compassionate vow, they do not regress.
Second, because the Buddha’s light constantly shines upon them.
First, the bodhicitta constantly increases and never regresses.
Third, the sounds of water birds, trees, and forests, as well as the resonance of wind and music,
all proclaim suffering and emptiness.
Those who hear [this] will constantly give rise to the mind that recollects the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Sangha, and therefore do not regress.
Fourth, that land consists entirely of bodhisattvas as virtuous friends;
there are no conditions for evil objects.
Externally, there are no ghosts, gods, or malevolent spirits;
internally, there are no three poisons or other afflictions.
Because afflictions ultimately do not arise, one does not regress.
Fifth, those born in that land have lifespans lasting for eternal kalpas;
because they are equal to the bodhisattvas and the Buddhas, they do not regress.
How much more so in this degenerate age,
where not only are these five conditions lacking,
but moreover, one encounters evil friends and associates.
Intoxicated and disordered by sounds and forms,
demons and devils confound the true;
the lifespan is short and fleeting.
These five types are all evil;
they obstruct and afflict the cultivation of the Path,
causing vast eons to pass in vain.
Please reflect upon this thoroughly.
Please reflect upon this thoroughly.
Someone said:
All dharmas are fundamentally without arising or ceasing;
they are equal, empty, and quiescent.
Why use forceful exhortation to urge one to abandon this and seek that?
The commentary states:
If it is said that seeking rebirth in the Western Paradise constitutes a violation of the principle of equality through the act of acceptance and rejection,
then you yourself are merely refuting that very attachment.
Is this not contrary to reason?
If you further argue that you do not seek birth there,
nor do you seek birth here;
This would then give rise to the view of annihilationism.
Does the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* not discourse on emptiness?
The Buddha cautioned Subhūti, saying:
"Do not entertain such a thought regarding those who have resolved to attain bodhicitta."
Regarding the Dharma, I do not speak of the characteristic of annihilation.
One who truly understands emptiness does so precisely within the context of dependent origination.

To realize that the nature of arising is non-arising and that the nature of cessation is non-cessation does not mean that they are annihilated into nothingness as something neither arising nor ceasing.
As the *Mūlamadhyamakakārikā* states:
"Those phenomena produced through causes and conditions—
I declare them to be empty.
I do not say they are empty after having been annihilated."
The Vimalakīrti Sūtra states:
"Although one knows that all Buddha-lands and sentient beings are empty,
one constantly cultivates the pure land."
To transform and guide all sentient beings.
Some say that the Pure Land resides within the mind.
Why must one seek elsewhere?
As the mind becomes pure, so too does the Buddha-land become pure.
Why then should one laboriously seek rebirth in a pure land in another direction?
The commentary states:
Furthermore, you do not properly understand the meaning of the "mind-ground" (*citta-bhūmi*).
You seem to believe that my mind is confined within the space of a single square inch.
One then sees the Western [Pure Land] situated far beyond the boundaries of this realm.
If this is indeed the case,
how can it be said that "if the mind is pure, then the Buddha-land is pure"?
The Avataṃsaka Sūtra says:
"Mind, Buddha, and sentient beings—
these three are without distinction."
Since the Buddha-dharma is all-pervasive,
the mind-dharma is likewise all-pervasive;
if they each possessed distinct directions, they would not be pervasive.
What is meant by "without differentiation"?
It is further said:
"The mind wanders through the Dharma-realm as if it were empty space."
How could space have any divisions?
If one understands that the single thought-moment is all-pervasive,
then even a single speck of dust is all-pervasive.
A hundred trillion lands are but a few steps away;
how could they exist outside the mind?
If worldly people were to discuss the principle of emptiness, [they would realize this].
One then dismisses cause and effect;
if one speaks only of one's own mind,
one fails to believe in the existence of external phenomena.
Is it not merely slandering the Dharma?
It is also slandering one's own mind, resulting in calamities that fall for ten thousand kalpas—
how truly lamentable!
To falsely create notions of right and wrong and obstruct others from attaining the Pure Land is the mark of a true evil teacher.
The *Sukhāvatīvyūha Sūtra* states:
The Buddha addressed Maitreya Bodhisattva, the devas, humans, and others:
"In the Land of Immeasurable Life, there are śrāvakas and bodhisattvas."
His merit and wisdom are beyond description;
his land is likewise so subtle, peaceful, blissful, and pure.
Why do you not strive to do good?
Contemplate the spontaneity of the Way;
each of you should constrain yourselves to exert diligence.
Strive to seek this for yourself;
you will surely attain transcendence and be reborn in the Land of Peace and Bliss.
The five evil paths and the miserable realms are naturally closed off by this horizontal cutting;
the ascending path is infinite,
easy to traverse yet unoccupied by people.
In that land there is no opposition;
one is naturally led [there].
Why not abandon worldly affairs?
By diligently practicing to seek the Way and its virtue,
one may attain ultimate longevity;
such life and bliss shall be without end.
I bow my head to the Buddhas of the ten directions, To Amitābha, the most honored among the holy,
To the Vaipulya Sūtras and the treasury of all Dharma-jewels,
And to Avalokiteśvara, Mahāsthāmaprāpta, And the assembly of Bodhisattvas of the great earth.
With a heart of sincere faith, I have carved woodblocks and printed ten thousand scrolls of the *Amitābha Sūtra*,
as well as ten thousand copies of the *Verse of Right Faith*,
each to be bestowed upon the fourfold assembly for their recitation and upholding.
The verses inspire faith, while the sūtras support recitation.
If one recites at least three fascicles each day, one will recite one thousand and eighty fascicles in a year;
in ten years, ten thousand and eight hundred.
How much more so for those who recite it many times and have practiced it over many years;
by thus accumulating merit, they will naturally be born before the Buddha.
Wherever these ten thousand scrolls of my sutras circulate, [may there be peace].
If even a single person, by reciting and upholding [this], attains birth in the Pure Land,
I vow that by the power of this merit, I shall certainly be born in that realm;
how much more so for many people, when the person has passed away but the scripture remains?
Transmitted and bestowed one after another, this is called the lamp of no end;
Lamp after lamp illuminates one another, shattering the long night of birth and death,
Revealing the Bodhi of the Buddhas, until all ultimately share in that same birth.
In the eternally quiescent and luminous Pure Land,
I take these pure merits and dedicate them to serve my sovereign and parents: may our nation’s sage emperors,
as well as sage queens, each enjoy ten thousand years of benevolent longevity.

Nurturing all classes of beings—my parents, kinsmen, enemies, and those who are neither—may they all, by virtue of these supreme roots of goodness, be born together in the Land of Peaceful Nurturing (Sukhāvatī).
The Verse of Old Lady Rìlún upon Seeing the Buddha, with Preface. Master Miaoxing, Fayi, [notes]: In the West, Amitābha Buddha possesses forty-eight vows.
The first [vow] says:
"When I attain Buddhahood,
may all sentient beings of the ten directions..."
If one desires to be born in my land and recites my name ten times, yet is not born there,
may I never attain enlightenment.
"I vow not to become a Buddha.
If a person, every morning at dawn, joins their palms facing west and recites the Buddha’s name ten times."
In this present life, calamities are averted and longevity is extended;
in the future, one will certainly attain rebirth there.
Behold the Qiantang [River] as an analogy for Amitābha.
This depicts the image of Amitābha Buddha within a solar disc as seen by the laywoman Yao Xingpo.
If a person can apply their mind with single-minded concentration,
then the response from the spiritual realm will likewise be such.
The Bhikṣu Miaoxing Fayi praised it with these verses:
"The Land of Ultimate Bliss has a specific location; It lies precisely where the sun sets every day."
Therefore, the Buddhist Vaidhīśī clearly contemplates the setting sun as if it were a suspended drum.
How excellent is this aged woman of the Yao clan, who is able to seek the Pure Land with such a mind!
For years she has gazed at it in the evening and contemplated it in the morning; in her practice and recollection, whether walking or sitting, she has forgotten both cold and heat.
Amitābha suddenly arises from the mind’s contemplation; In a moment of daze, he clearly beholds him again.
At that time, the void is utterly free of even a trace of cloud; The sun still lingers in the west, driven by the charioteer Xihe.
The Buddha-sun blazes forth, surpassing the brilliance of the sun; His deep blue eyes and jade-like *ūrṇā* mark his wondrous features.
My eyes were startled and my heart filled with joy and sorrow; I ran to inform the Teacher, Maitreya, recounting in detail all that I had seen—truly marvelous.
I prayed, "I wish to depict your golden countenance upon silk and brush.
Having heard of this supreme event, I marveled at its rarity and spoke these verses to awaken those who have not yet understood.
Know that you are not far from the Buddha; this is why even those of icchantika nature can attain it.
Though one may pass through ten trillion lands, in a single thought-moment one transcends them as if taking a single step.
If a deluded person asks for the way, point the path to them: "Go straight ahead like this."

Eulogy and Simile for Amitābha: A Eulogy and Simile for Amitābha, with Preface. Ding Zhu, Grand Master of the Left for Consultation on State Affairs, renounced his wife and slaves to become a follower of the Tathāgata.
He recruited ten thousand people to establish a Pure Land assembly.
A local man, Ding Zhu, praised him with this verse:
"The mind is pure, and thus the Buddha-land is pure; The Dharma King does not speak falsely."
Having pulled oneself out from the dust and defilements, one has already beheld the lotus within the fire.
When not a single thought arises or ceases, the Land of Ultimate Bliss appears before one;
the great trichiliocosm shares this same realm—how could it be limited to the karmic conditions of ten thousand people?

Vaidhīṣikā again prostrated herself and entreated the Muni: "Please explain the causes for the pure retribution of the Western Land— the sixteen contemplations together with the three pure karmas; by practicing these, one shall attain rebirth there.
Sitting upright and facing west, contemplate the solar disc: visualize the sun about to set, like a suspended drum."
Having seen this, while closing and opening one's eyes, one should cause the mind to dwell firmly upon what is clearly manifest.
Next, one should form the visualization of water and see the western direction as entirely a pure land.
Once the water has been visualized, imagine it turning into ice, shining brilliantly and transparently like a ground of lapis lazuli.
When one correctly contemplates the lapis lazuli ground, one clearly and distinctly perceives the Land of Ultimate Bliss;
eight kinds of pure breezes play the sounds of music, performing melodies on suffering, emptiness, non-self, and impermanence.
One beholds the fourfold rows of jeweled trees, seven layers deep, and jeweled flowers blooming within wondrous palaces.
The shadows of jeweled banners and canopies overlap in layers, Within which the Buddha-lands of the ten directions appear.

In the five-fold pure lands are ponds of the seven treasures; The waters within these ponds possess the eight meritorious qualities, Flowing forth while proclaiming the names of the Buddha, Dharma, and Sangha. Therein are wondrous jewel lotuses, numbering in the thousands of millions.
A land of myriad jewels with jeweled pavilions, Jeweled trees interspersed with lotus ponds;
When this general visualization is accomplished, It is called the coarse perception of that Sukhāvatī.
The wondrous lotus pedestal and throne, Vastly formed through Amitābha’s power of vows—

When forming this visualization, the mind remains undistracted. One should visualize with concentration the birth within the Land of Ultimate Bliss of the various Buddhas and Tathāgatas, whose bodies are the Dharmadhātu, pervading all perceptions of sentient beings.
The wise should contemplate this visualized mind; this very mind is the image of the Buddha and the Bodhisattvas.
The golden body of Amitāyus Buddha radiates light that universally illumines all classes of sentient beings;
those who diligently practice and fix their minds on contemplation shall see all Buddhas appear before them and bestow upon them the same prophecy.
The Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara possesses a body of purple-gold, with a tuft of hair between his eyebrows the color of the seven treasures.
Radiant light streams forth, filling the ten directions; within that light, countless billions of transformation Buddhas appear.
Next, one beholds the body of Bodhisattva Śrīkṣitigarbha (Potuoshizhi), whose dimensions are equal to those of Avalokiteśvara and no different.
Only within the jeweled flask upon his uṣṇīṣa do all manner of lights gather to manifest the deeds of the Buddha.
Visualize clearly that your body is born in the Land of Ultimate Bliss; The lotus flower closes, and you dwell within it.
As the flower opens, you see Buddhas filling the void of space, And water-birds and forest trees proclaim the verses of the Dharma.
Visualize again Amitābha and his two Bodhisattvas, Manifesting supernatural powers and transformations as described before.
Amassing these merits brings immeasurable blessings; Through meditative concentration, one is born in Sukhāvatī to serve the Golden Sage.
With a compassionate heart, refrain from killing and uphold the various precepts;
Recite the Mahāyāna Vaipulya sūtras, practice the six recollections, and dedicate these merits toward the vow. At the moment of death, the transformed Buddhas will all come to welcome you.
It is not necessary to uphold the Vaipulya sutras; To understand the primary truth is to clarify cause and effect.
When the golden lotus pedestal appears at the time of death, One sees one’s own body seated upon that pedestal.
Deeply believe in cause and effect and honor the Mahāyāna; Simply give rise to the aspiration for supreme bodhi.
By this merit, may I vow to be reborn there; having been born, may I dwell upon the Ground of Joy (*pramuditā-bhūmi*).

Upholding the five precepts, the eight precepts, and the fast, and practicing all the various moralities, may I dedicate these merits with the vow that at the end of my life I be born there to hear the sound of the Dharma, and may I immediately attain Arhatship at that very moment.
If a person, with a sincere heart, for one day and one night, observes the precepts and the fast without breach or flaw,

and dedicates this merit toward rebirth— Practicing filial piety toward one's parents and acting with benevolence and righteousness— one shall encounter a virtuous friend at the moment of death, And upon the blossoming of the seven-day lotus, receive the prediction of enlightenment.
The causes of Amitābha’s great vows are explained at length: In the time it takes to bend and extend an arm, one is born in that land.

If a person, though not slandering the honored sutras, Has committed various evil deeds without shame or remorse, Should they encounter exhortation to mind Amitābha at the end of life, They will be born there and attain the first stage (*bhūmi*) after ten kalpas.
If there are sentient beings who violate the various precepts, Who steal the property of the Sangha or the Three Jewels,
And at the moment of death encounter exhortation to recite Amitābha’s name— In the space of a single thought-moment, they shall be born in that land.
Even those who have committed the five heinous crimes or the ten evil deeds, And should have fallen into hell to undergo all manner of suffering, [shall likewise be reborn there].
If, at the moment of death, one encounters exhortation to recite the name of Amitābha, one will certainly transcend birth in that land.
When the form of the setting sun resembles a suspended drum, sit upright in the full-lotus posture facing west;
though the body has not yet reached the Lotus Pond, the mind is first sent back to the Land of Ultimate Bliss.
Visualizing water as ice, utterly pure, Manifesting as a ground of lapis lazuli with jeweled banners held aloft,
its radiance shining like a thousand suns— This is called the accomplishment of the water-visualization of the meditative mind;
when the jewel-ground is adorned and flowers rain down, One should contemplate the beautiful banners, pennants, and pavilions.
The level ground is the mind; the myriad phenomena are its conditions. Relying on objects to clarify the mind, it cannot be moved.
Layer upon layer, precious trees lean against one another in height; Adorned with jeweled nets reaching through several layers of the sky.
If one can realize that all is but the state of mind, Though one be in the Western Land, the path is not far.
The eight virtues are clear and still, known as the Pool of Virtue; Its golden sand floor shines with radiant brilliance.
As the flowing water recites verses on non-arising, Those who hear them contemplate the mind and collect their thoughts.
In this Land Adorned with Jewels, the seven treasures are perfected; Within its towers and pavilions, celestial music resounds.
The jeweled trees and lotus ponds are named Universal Contemplation; The contemplation of their radiance extinguishing transgressions is no small matter.
The lotus has eighty-four thousand petals, Adorned with myriad wonders and countless rays of light.
Using this lotus as a precious throne, It blooms in wait for the King of Dharma to sit upon it.
While the wisdom that perceives the Buddha’s true body has not yet opened, first cause yourself to visualize him seated upon a lotus pedestal;
the bodies of Buddhas and Bodhisattvas fill that land—understand that these images come from nowhere.
That Buddha’s majestic, exalted, and supreme body emits light that shines everywhere, as numerous as motes of dust.
Sentient beings, receiving his illumination, turn their hearts toward the Buddha; they are the people of the Western Pure Land.
This Bodhisattva is named Avalokiteśvara, whose great compassionate heart universally covers the ten directions.
With the majestic spiritual power of a mass of purple-gold light, he vows to guide and receive sentient beings with a depth as vast as the ocean.
The Unsurpassed Power is named Mahāsthāmaprāpta; Pure, Wondrous, and Bright, he is titled Amitābha.
If a person contemplates these two Bodhisattvas, They shall not dwell within the foul and filthy sac of a womb.
When the time for universal observation arrives, they will achieve merit; Visualize their bodies entering the clusters of wondrous flowers in the West.
The lotus flowers are clearly seen opening and closing; Bodhisattvas and Tathāgatas fill the azure sky.
The Buddhas manifest majestic light in bodies both large and small, With Avalokiteśvara and Mahāsthāmaprāpta as their companions.
If one accomplishes this through mixed visualization, This is also called the "Cause of Purity."

The upper grade is divided into three ranks based on depth: at the end of life, the Buddhas bestow their light and welcome them onto lotus pedestals to be born in An-yang (Sukhāvatī). Know this to be the Perfect Teaching;
among the ten levels of faith, those of the middle grade are persons of the five ranks who externally cultivate the restraint of precepts and internally cultivate the truth.
At the end of life, one transcends the five realms of existence; One immediately attains the untainted body of the Western Land.

Though ordinary beings may have created manifold karmas, If they once contemplate and visualize the Name by the side of the Lotus Pond at sunset, They will be born in the Pure Land in this very life. Know that this is neither easy nor difficult.

Verses on the Sixteen Contemplations. By the Vinaya Master Yuanzhao of Great Wisdom. At the assembly on Mount Gṛdhrakūṭa, when the assembly on Mount Gṛdhrakūṭa had dispersed, [the teaching] emerged from within the royal palace.
When the business was concluded, he returned home.
Ānanda recounted it once more:
"Vaidhī requested the Dharma while confined within the inner palace."
You have initiated this great undertaking;
the sentient beings of this turbid and evil age now receive its benefits.
1. First Daily Contemplation: On the first day, contemplate the setting sun like a suspended drum;
it marks the path out of birth and death throughout the twelve periods of the day.
Fixing the mind on a single point:
Second, the Contemplation of Water. One visualizes a great body of water, clear and limpid;
it becomes still and solidifies into ice.
The lapis lazuli ground is manifest, transparent both inside and out.
Third, the contemplation of the ground: regarding the contemplation of the lapis lazuli ground.
Adorning all marks,
clearly seeing and discerning them,
removing doubts and breaking through obstructions.
4. The Fourth Meditation on Trees: The trees in this meditation grow in seven layers.
Nets of pearls and flowered palaces provide a clear, cool shade that hangs down and spreads everywhere.
Exquisite and boundless.
Fifth, the contemplation of the ponds: contemplating the eight ponds of virtuous waters, with the wondrous colors of the seven treasures.
The lotus blooms and the birds sing;
they wash away all afflictions and delusions.
6. The Sixth General Contemplation: Celestial Music in the Pavilion Above.
Praising the Buddha, Dharma, and Sangha;
the jewel trees, the ground, and the ponds are all perfectly accomplished in a single thought-moment.
Seventh, the contemplation of the seat: contemplate the great lotus seat,
adorned with a hundred jewels,
subtle and inconceivable.
Through the power of Dharmakara’s vows,
in the eighth contemplation of the image: the image relies upon the form, yet when the true nature is concentrated,
one perceives the truth and forgets the image.
The Three Sages shine brilliantly, yet they are still termed "coarse conceptions. 9.
The Ninth Meditation on the Buddha: Contemplating the Buddha’s Marks and Signs.
Once the essential core of this sutra is realized and samādhi manifests before one,
only then does one come to know its profound subtlety.
10. Contemplating Avalokiteśvara: Contemplating Avalokiteśvara, one beholds his light illuminating the five realms of existence.
The Buddha stands upon his crown;
by hearing his name, one obtains merit.
How much more so when one contemplates them with clarity!
11. The Eleven Contemplations of Śrīkūṭa: Śrīkūṭa’s light shines upon all Buddhas, and his power rescues all beings from suffering.
The light from the crown-vase fills and universally manifests throughout all Buddha-lands.
12. Universal Contemplation: Universally contemplating while seated cross-legged upon a lotus.
The lotus flowers open and close;
both the primary and secondary adornments are fully encompassed therein.
13. Miscellaneous Contemplations: Thirteen miscellaneous contemplations stand prominently above the pond.
A sixteen-foot image manifests in various sizes.
There is absolutely no fixed characteristic.
Chapter 14: The Highest Grade of the Highest Birth. In the highest grade of the highest birth, the three minds are fully developed, and the profound principle of truth is clearly understood.
The golden platform follows him as he departs,
and he immediately realizes the non-arising of dharmas.
Those of the highest grade among those born by middle capacity realize the emptiness of all phenomena.
There will be no agitation whatsoever;
one will be reborn immediately upon making the vow,
without the necessity of recitation.
Regarding those of the lower grade within the superior class: they merely give rise to the aspiration for the Way but have not yet fathomed the subtle principles;
it is only upon reaching that [Pure Land] that they attain illumination.
Receiving the prophecy of attaining *bodhi*.
15. The Fifteen Middle Grades: Upper Birth in the Middle Grade. Those who have long maintained the various precepts will be reborn according to their wishes.
Having heard the teaching on suffering and emptiness,
they attain arhatship;
those born in the middle grade of the middle birth remain there for one day and one night.
By reverently upholding the precepts and making vows and aspirations,
one shall behold the Buddha as the lotus blossoms and immediately enter the stream of the sages.
Regarding those of the lower grade within the middle level of rebirth: they are filial, fraternal, benevolent, and compassionate;
their understanding is awakened, and they encounter two Bodhisattvas.
Hearing the Dharma, they attain deliverance.
16. Lower Grade, Part 1: Those born in the upper part of the lower grade who, throughout their lives, accumulated evil, but upon death encountered a virtuous teacher.
By reciting the Buddha’s name even once,
one is born in a lotus pond;
this is the "Middle Birth of the Lower Grade" (the second of the three middle grades), for those whose transgressions against the precepts are deep.
As the fires of hell approached him from all sides,
he heard the Dharma and turned his mind [toward enlightenment];
the assembly of holy ones then came to welcome him away.
For those of the lowest-of-the-low grade who have committed the ten evil deeds and the five heinous crimes,
and are oppressed by suffering at the moment of death, one should teach them the practice of ten recitations of the Buddha's name.
The flowers bloom with a golden hue;
gradually, the skin becomes like that of a rooster and the hair turns white like a crane’s. Watch as the gait grows increasingly unsteady and faltering.
Even if one were to fill the halls with gold and jade, who could escape decay, decrepitude, aging, and illness?
Let you enjoy a thousand forms of happiness, yet impermanence will inevitably arrive;
there is only the path of cultivation, which consists simply in reciting the name of Amitābha Buddha.
The three realms blaze fiercely like a mass of fire; for the practitioner, they are not yet a place of rest.
The Lotus Superior Friend has waited for a long time; Gather your body and mind well, and return home.
Visualize his holy form with your eyes and keep it in your heart; In every thought-moment, you must not give rise to doubt.
In years to come, when you stand at the gate of the lotus in the Pure Land, Remember this time of reciting the Buddha’s name in Saṃsāra.
The Land of Ultimate Bliss is not separate from the true Dharmadhātu; Amitābha is none other than the sovereign of one’s own mind.
The tuft of white hair between his brows has no fixed location; even a pillar and a lantern emit radiance.
Diligently cultivate the precepts of fasting without delay; a thousand sages have together opened the gate of mindfulness of the Buddha.
Once the task is accomplished, one returns to the Pure Land, Enveloped by the white tuft of light to serve the Compassionate Honored One.
The many joys of the Western Paradise are vast and profound, difficult to proclaim even through aeons;
The span of his life is never-ending, and how could his radiance have any limit?
The wind of the Way blows through the green spikenard; The water of concentration brings forth red lotuses.
In this ocean assembly where all flow to the source, Celestial flowers fall before the seat.
The multitude of disciples are all pure; The path to Bodhi is easily realized.
Every thought is right mindfulness; every object accords with the True Vehicle.
The nature-ground is as brilliant as lapis lazuli, and the perfect sound resonates like the songs of myriad birds.
You must surely ascend to the shore of enlightenment; do not allow yourself to follow after the city of doubt.
With feet treading the ground of sorrowlessness, The body dwells in the land beyond aging.
Six times a day one pays homage to the Holy Lord; At the break of dawn, one departs for other realms.
The precious palace follows the body, And celestial flowers and incense fill the lands.
Returning, one dwells again in the original abode; how long can the flavor of dhyāna-joy last?
Do not say that the Western Land is far away; the Western Land is right before one's eyes.
Although it passes beyond a hundred thousand [yojanas], it has never been separated from the three thousand [worlds].
As soon as one opens the mouth to recite the Buddha’s name, A lotus has already been planted in the pond of the mind.
If faith does not regress, One will certainly pay homage to the Golden Immortal (the Buddha).
The pond gathers the waters of merit; The wind stirs the sounds of pipes and strings.
Latticed nets veil the realm of space; Towers and pavilions reflect the jeweled groves.
The six sense organs are ever in harmony with the Way; The myriad phenomena are realized as being solely mind.
It is not that others find it difficult to reach; It is entirely because one’s faith is not yet deep.
The classes of practitioners are divided into three grades; Together they share a single lotus pond.
Once one has ascended to Sukhāvatī, One will certainly attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
When the obstructions are exhausted and the sun of radiance shines forth, The mind opens and one beholds the Buddha.
Within this, there is infinite joy; only those who walk the same path know it.
The principle of True Suchness is the Land of Ultimate Bliss;
When deluded, one sinks into this world; Upon awakening, one goes to the West.
The vast cycle of saṃsāra ceases, and one’s life span becomes far-reaching and long.
If the root of faith arises for even a single thought-moment, the mind-ground has already become cool and refreshing.
Those with deep faith will surely proceed [to liberation], while those with much doubt cannot yet be known.
With a pure mind relying on a single thought, One's merit and practice transcend incalculable eons (*asaṃkhyeya-kalpa*).
Thus one is ranked among those of non-retrogression (*avaivartika*), And may likewise advance in cultivation as one destined for succession (*abhiṣeka-bhūmi*).
One should be courageous and diligent; There is no need to wait for a long time.

When people ask about those of the Chan school: If one forgets all worldly affairs through the Gate of the Patriarchs, And is already able to transcend the Land of Ultimate Bliss, Why must one go to the West?
Yet upon hearing the words of the Chan school, One realizes that the West is one's own native land.
Aśvaghoṣa personally instructed and exhorted us, and Nāgārjuna likewise praised this;
do not speak of the sufferings of Sahā. The sufferings of Sahā kill people;
greed, hatred, and delusion disturb the mind, and skin, flesh, and blood constitute the body.
The rākṣasas dwell in caves of hatred and enmity; the aggregates and sense-bases are a village of ignorance.
One must surely ascend to the Land of Ultimate Bliss; do not be negligent on the path home.
Do not speak of the sufferings of Saṃsāra—yet the sufferings of Saṃsāra are the deepest.
Demons constantly act as companions, And illnesses perpetually invade.
In this realm of sensual desire and licentiousness, With a mind of serene detachment through dhyāna, One must surely ascend to Sukhāvatī; Do not hesitate on the path home.
Do not speak of the sufferings of Sahā, which cause tears to flow in profusion;
The three calamities revolve within the wheel, and one is scorched by the fires of the five pains.
The radiance of the Śāla trees is forever shrouded, and the assembly at the Dragon Flower is still far off.
One must surely ascend to the Land of Ultimate Bliss; do not shun the toil on the path home.
Do not speak of the sufferings of Saṃsāra. Vaidhī said to the World-Honored One:
"In this kalpa of the defilement of afflictions, my child cries out against his unborn enemy."
How perverse was the mind of Devadatta! King Bimbisāra’s resentment cannot be discussed;
he shall surely ascend to the Land of Ultimate Bliss. Such evil has never been heard of before.
If a person wishes to be born in the Peaceful Nurturing Land, the wise should cause them to cultivate the practice of visualization.
The true body of Amitābha is difficult to contemplate; those of initial resolve should first contemplate carved or painted images.
When the mental image is perfected, the eye of wisdom opens; the golden-hued body is as clear as one's own palm.
In a single thought-moment, one can cross the five evil realms; who would say there is no way to make the journey easy?
Ten thousand people with one mind recite the name of Amitābha; Through the mutual support of their collective power, their vows become manifold.
When a single lotus blooms and they behold the Buddha face-to-face, Only then do they realize that the Pure Land surpasses this Sahā world.
The trees, the waters, and the birds each proclaim the Dharma; The jeweled nets and golden terraces are all sites of enlightenment.
If you can understand the tolling of the bell and the beating of the drum, Amitābha emits rays of light everywhere.
Yet as your hair and beard grow white with frost, the monkey-mind and horse-will remain wild and unruly.
One day, when you close your eyes to depart this world, you will realize for the first time that the years in the hells are long indeed.
The retributions of karma differ, and circumstances are not the same; In this weary life, there is no ground for escaping the cage.
If you wish to know the Amitābha Buddha of your own nature, He resides within your single thought-moment of morning and evening.
The ocean of suffering and the pit of karma for sentient beings are deep; Those who do not believe in causes and conditions sink and drown for long.

Only when you hear the sound again will you recite the Buddha’s name; Only then will you know that the "old woman's heart" regarding wife and children is not the mountain monk’s talk of right and wrong. You must know that these are the demonic affairs of practice;
You must urgently tread upon the soles of your straw sandals And pass through the pool of the five desires of this Sahā world.
A Verse Presented to the Laywoman Chen Xingpo, with Preface The Master Ciben Facong was visiting the laywoman Xingpo.
When he arrived, the Master asked her how long she had been practicing cultivation.
The old woman replied that she had practiced for many years.
The Master asked if she had ever seen Ānanda;
she replied that she had often encountered spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra*).
The Master asked, "How do you instruct others?
He replied,
"Directly pointing to the source."
He neither reads the sutras nor recites the Buddha's name.
The Master said:
It was because he had spoken erroneously that [the woman] was converted. Once she was convinced,
he then showed her two verses.
Directly cut through to the root; there is no need for cultivation. Considered from the start, these words have little basis.
One must grasp the fundamental to escape birth and death; In every thought-moment, recite Amitābha’s name—do not seek it elsewhere.
Reciting the Buddha’s name and reading the sutras are the essential journey; One must believe that from the beginning, water has always been ice.
Only by deeply investigating the source from its root, Can each utterance be raised with perfect clarity.
Hearing it said that the Western Land is most easily sought, All myriad conditions cease at once from this point on.
With prayer beads in hand and feet crossed upon a round mat, One simply acts as the head of Amitābha.
Listening to the teachings and practicing *chan* while seeking outwardly, One has never once turned back to reflect with deep contemplation.
As the light of the eyes is about to fall and the path ahead grows dark, Only then does one realize that all one’s life was spent using the mind in error.
Śākyamuni praised the Western Land as it truly is; The transcendence of both the environment and its inhabitants reveals his intent.
With faith and aspiration, hold the Name without other thoughts; With every sound, let the mind dwell upon the light of the white curl between the brows.
Through cultivation over kalpas as numerous as motes of dust, one achieves a body of merit and virtue, Establishing a glorious name of boundless radiance and longevity.
Because of this, every Buddha offers praise; How could we not raise our voices?
The Four-Character Great Name was proclaimed from the Golden Mouth; Success is achieved solely through the firmness of one’s own mind.
This divine method is simple and rare indeed. With a single wipe of the hand, one joyfully dwells upon the precious lotus.
*Verses on the Essential Heart of Mindfulness of the Buddha*, with Preface, by Dhyāna Master Daoyin of Cao’an. Expounded by Śākyamuni Tathāgata.
Amitābha Buddha is the Dharma-realm body (*dharmadhātu-kāya*).
Furthermore, the Tiantai master Zhiyi stated that his essence is the true aspect (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*).
Relying on these two teachings as the essential core of the mind,
then across ten million billion lands,
As if gazing into a clear mirror,
I have composed this humble verse to reflect upon my own mind.
Is there anyone with true discernment who can rejoice in this?
The boundless oceans of lands encompass the ocean of space; this ocean of space is entirely the Lotus Palace.
Throughout the Lotus Palaces, the ocean of space is all-pervasive; within this ocean of space, the countenance of Amitābha alone is revealed.

Amitābha Buddha is neither born nor extinguished; Like the moon in water, difficult to grasp and difficult to seize, he is utterly beyond words of separation. Such is his body, such is his responsive resonance, and such is his teaching.
I and Amitābha are fundamentally not two; Only when deluded awareness secretly arises do they suddenly appear as distinct.
From now on, I shall sweep away all dust of both emptiness and existence; Father and son, by nature, meet once more.
I vow to cultivate the three blessings and diligently practice the six mindfulnesses, So that my actions of body, speech, and mind remain free from blemish.
Now, through this mindfulness of Amitābha, I shall never grow weary until I behold him face to face.
Eulogy on the Carving of a Fragrant Image of Amitābha, with Preface. By the Dharma Master Ke’guan of Jiěkōng, of Siming Huxi.
There was a practitioner named Fànqín who received his training at Chóngjiào Monastery.
By the power of his long-accumulated vows,
he came to enter the meditation hall of Yanqing Temple to perform the Samantabhadra Repentance.
While reciting the Lotus Sutra,
he felt someone rub the crown of his head in the darkness, though he was unaware of it himself;
he dedicated this merit toward rebirth in the Western Paradise.
He increased his cultivation of the *nien-fo* samādhi and carved an image of Amitābha Buddha from red sandalwood;
it was like the moon reflected in water, utterly ungraspable.
He sought out Laozhu Hermitage and requested that [the Master] act as his witness;
there was nothing else to bring forth.
This alone is it: the white jade-like luminous hair is my own mind; the purple-gold radiant marks are my own nature’s radiance.
These cannot be attained as separate entities at once; directly, there is nothing that is not the wondrous, supreme samādhi.
A thousand-petaled lotus net wrapped in emptiness;
In a dream, treading upon a pond of seven-jeweled flowers, one finds the ground of the Western Return secure. Not a single speck of doubt remains:
originally having no home, where is there to return? Who knows that along this path at the edge of the clouds?
The mountain stream’s light flickers as the moon rises over the western peaks; This is precisely the moment when dreams of the immortal pool are severed.

The waters of merit in the seven-jeweled pond, And the Dharma-sounds of birds throughout the six periods of the day— Enveloped by the interlacing light of compassion, free from demonic affliction, They soar with ease, beyond birth and death.
The pavilions and towers adorn the golden realm; Lotuses are fragrant and pure, with the radiant light of jewels.
Those who encounter flower garlands and jeweled necklaces All say it is born from recollecting the Buddha.
How bitter, how bitter—truly bitter indeed! Why do you wander aimlessly and refuse to turn back?
The compassionate father grieves in the Jade Hall, Wishing to pass on the family legacy, awaiting your return.
Come back! Come back! In the Pure Land of the West, white lotuses bloom;
Arisen gusts of fragrant wind cannot disperse them. On the purple-gold terrace, one dwells in carefree joy.
Venerating Amitābha while within Amitābha, at every step transcending Saṃsāra;
Even a Buddha cannot attain Buddhahood—whence could a Māra arise?
Worldly affairs are but a single dream; among all people, who shall live for a hundred years?
In every thought-moment, recite the name of Amitābha Buddha; A precious lotus blooms within the pond.
As for the affairs of this physical life in the world, what are they? They are like spring swallows busily building their nests;
Toiling and striving to manage a household— It is not as good as reciting the name of Amitābha according to one's capacity.
With brilliant prose and eloquent debate, one may attain a high rank; In crimson and purple robes, one’s body is honored and one’s spirit is full.
Yet when office is high, who can avoid the arrival of impermanence? It is better to employ skillful means and recite the name of Amitābha.
Flying spears and running arrows—such momentum is hard to withstand; A fine steed galloping forth is as swift as a shuttle.
To possess strength rivaling ten thousand men yet succumb to old age and illness is not as good as practicing wholesome thoughts of Amitābha;
To have wealth and resources that one never tires of, yet anxiously calculating morning and night for fear of error,
so that one does not realize one’s hair has turned white from worry and distress, is not as good as being contented and mindful of Amitābha.
With a clear and resonant voice, you sing songs well; A single new verse, its melody harmonious.
Even if your singing could cause the drifting clouds to fall, It would not equal the purity of reciting Amitābha’s name with a clean mouth.
With willow-leaf brows and star-like eyes, you rival the Goddess of the Moon; Your jade-like body is ever fresh, clad in fine silks and brocades.
The beauty of one's countenance may only last through youth; It is better to contemplate Amitābha early on.
In chess, one boasts of many strategies against rival states; Yet in the scramble for the "capture," one first neglects self-refinement.
Half of one's life is thus wasted; It is better to sit upright and contemplate Amitābha.
The merchant broker is most restless, traveling everywhere to distant lands and foreign regions;
amidst the perils of wind and waves upon the rivers and lakes, it is better to return home and recite the name of Amitābha.
Those who are adept at public office exploit and ruin others, skillfully fabricating lawsuits and flaunting their thuggish power.
As family wealth gradually dissipates, it invites resentment; It is better to reduce complications and recite the name of Amitābha.
Killing brings karma and enemies, and debts gradually multiply; With what words or reasoning will you face Yama?
I teach you the Dharma for transcending this life along a single path: It is better to recognize your remorse and recite the name of Amitābha.
The Dharma-Treasury grew up within the royal palace; Cultivating the Way, he departed from the city gates.
He made forty-eight vows, Vast aspirations to rescue all living beings.
How wondrous is this Pure Land! All who come are the very cream of humanity.
How can one rely on faltering words? One must surely set out at dawn, riding upon transformation.
The subtle function lies herein: traversing existence and surveying non-existence. The spirit proceeds from obscurity to penetration;
through consciousness, the coarse is illuminated. By accumulating the minute, one draws oneself forward; though based on effort, the root is emptiness.
Effacing those three contemplations and forgetting this subtle remainder, one enters a state of profound stillness. How could there be a beginning?
Treading the Mysterious and penetrating the Subtle, one melts away until even the sense of "fitting" is forgotten. Thus, the numinous radiance expands;
the mind roams through vast domains, reaching a point where it need not tread upon the mechanisms of action, employing them instead with emptiness.
Gathering them through the rarefied, the divine form is as naturally concentrated as the heavens. Rounding and reflecting like morning clouds, it merges with transformation;
it dwells among all things as one of their multitude. It responds without fixed form, yet those who receive it distinguish themselves for themselves.
In a mere instant, the profound mirror reflects the swirling dust of gold and water.
Reflecting upon my entire life, my innate wisdom and insight have long been entrusted to those of lofty and profound character, so that I might rely on their hidden power;
I intend to transform this noble merit into something unfathomably deep.
This thought arose within me, and I focused my mind upon the Western Realm. From the *Lushan Ji* (Collection from Mount Lu).
**Preface to the Verses on the Samādhi of Buddha-Recollection** The Master of Repentance, Ciyun Zunshe, wrote this preface:
"The samādhi of Buddha-recollection is the wondrous path for realizing sainthood."
For all those who strive to advance within the stream of the Dharma,
how could there be any path that does not proceed by way of this?
Master Huiyuan of the Jin dynasty—
He transformed the assembly of the worthy at Xunyang,
establishing it as a model for reaching the ultimate limit;
so too did Wang Qiao of Langya and the multitude of sages.
These were all poems on the *Nianfo Sanmei* (Samādhi of Buddha-Recollection).
Huiyuan composed a preface for them.
In the *Bingshen* year of the Huangsong dynasty, the śramaṇa Zunshe gathered more than a hundred noble guests from Shaming to assemble [this collection].
During one day and one night each during the two middle months of spring and winter,
he gathered at the Baoyun Lecture Hall to contemplate the Immeasurable Buddha and recite the scriptures of the Han and Wei periods.
In the year of Renyin, after the [throne] had been abdicated, I went to Mount Dongsan in Taizhou;
suddenly, I thought of how what had just occurred would soon become a thing of the past.
Regrettably, there is no record of this;
therefore, I have composed a poem in the style of the worthy men of the Jin dynasty and inscribed it upon the stone.
To be transmitted to future generations. The poem has four stanzas and eight lines.
Ten thousand emotions transcend the physical form; solemn and still is the empty hall.
Subtle brilliance surpasses all colors; the profound spirit provides the beginning and continues the succession.

Letting go as it drifts, the boat passes south of the water.
There is no need to seek fellow practitioners elsewhere.
The Amitābha Buddha within one’s own home;
in every thought-moment, the utpala flower blooms.
The boat is steered by the celestial wind toward the North.
Wind-swept marshes and moonlit islets reflect the light of the mind;
suddenly, shifting my thoughts, I enter the Land of Common Abode,
unaware that my entire being has boarded a lotus-leaf vessel.
The boat sails toward the east, west, south, and north;
yet, as before, it does not leave the ancient sandbar.
Suddenly, one turns the rudder of empty space.
The fragrance fills the boat and the flowers fill the vessel;
if one does not set sail, one remains at home,
allowing the three carts to be dragged outside the gate.
Laughing, I gaze into the depths of the burning house;
upon dry land, pure water-lilies bloom.
This ready-made koan is beyond all deliberation.
The dawn bells strike repeatedly as the wax candles burn long;
throughout the six periods of day and night, the sound never ceases.
A fragrant breeze carries the scent of white lotuses to fill the entire gate.
With Buddha in mind, one directs the mind toward recollection;
when the mind reaches emptiness, even Buddha is forgotten.
Casting off all attachments and returning home, one examines once more.
Flowers bloom in red, white, blue, and yellow;
the mind of mindfulness follows like a shadow its form.
Whether in stillness or clamor, leisure or toil, it never pauses.
Breaking through the physical form, shadow and body vanish;
in the Western Heaven and this land, all paths are cut off.
At dawn and dusk, perform prostrations and repentance.
Bowing my head, I weep and address the Venerable Amitābha:
"How many times have I wandered through the six realms of rebirth?
I vow that this time, I shall finally escape the net."
Supporting him out, he reveals the red *uṣṇīṣa* atop his head;
sweeping away the void, he displays the white *ūrṇā-kośa* radiance within his brow.
"Amitābha Buddha," he utters with a resonant voice.
The cycle of saṃsāra through kalpas of eons is forgotten in a single thought;
upon the ground of golden sand there are no red lotuses;
within this mass of flesh lies the Most Honored One.
Taking a single step from atop the crowns of a thousand sages,
one casually kicks down the gate of nirvana;
six donkeys pull a single cart.
After the rain, the muddy roads are even more treacherous;
Amitābha Buddha’s compassionate heart is most urgent,
urging me on with the whip of sorrow as I strive to reach my home.
To mind Amitābha Buddha, there is no hardship;
to enter the holy and transcend the mundane, it takes but a single snap of the fingers.
Cast aside all else but Amitābha, and maintain right mindfulness.
All manner of things heard and seen are mutually unrelated;
do not discriminate between right and wrong, and cease seeking out affairs.
Should you encounter further complications, let your mind be without fear.
Constantly associating with the King of Vows, one cannot be invaded by hundreds of thousands of demonic afflictions.
Amitābha went westward; the Patriarch came from the West.
Reciting the Buddha’s name and practicing Zen share the same essence;
the mass of doubt accumulated over kalpas is shattered as the flower of the mind blooms together in the same way.
The lecture hall divides the schools of Characteristics and Nature;
one establishes characteristics while the other refutes them—thus they do not accord.
Now that we have come to this flower pond, let us speak.
How could the lotus buds ever be anything but red?
The Buddhist monastic robe maintains the pure precepts;
Yet the Vinaya says that the five precepts have not yet been fully cultivated.
Who would have known that within the six-word True Sutra,
the eighty thousand majestic deportments are gathered in a single phrase?
The Buddhas of the six directions extend their broad and long tongues.
All praise those who practice mindfulness of the Buddha in this Sahā world;
one must believe that in the world of the white lotus,
there is never a time when the springtime of the kalpa-jar does not flourish.
The earth shook and heaven was startled as he diligently recited the Buddha’s name;
knocking at gates and pounding on doors, he exhorted others to practice.
When asked why he acted in such a manner, he replied: [Because I am seeking liberation].
Fearing that sentient beings would fall into the fiery pit,
he attained Buddhahood this very day;
even the Master of the Land of Bliss considered it too late.
If one can still desire further existence,
one will surely be lost in the cycle of saṃsāra forever;
yet, reciting the Buddha’s name does not hinder daily life.
In daily life, people obstruct one another;
who can preserve this phantom of a hundred-year illusion?
Do not fail the King of Vows from the Western Heaven.
Those who possess wealth and honor should appropriately recite the Buddha's name.
With gold filling their treasuries and grain overflowing their granaries,
they shall enjoy worldly abundance without deficiency.
Only lacking the sight of the King of Vows at the moment of death.
When a person in poverty recites the Buddha’s name,
they have no household affairs to occupy their thoughts.
Naked and bare-handed, he ascends directly to claim a branch upon the lotus flower;
in his old age, reciting the Buddha’s name is precisely what is appropriate.
The days until your departure are not many; do not forget this for even a moment.
"Namo Amitābha," these six characters are called the compassionate vessel that crosses the sea of suffering.
The common saying is that it is difficult for the young to practice mindfulness of the Buddha;
I say that youth is precisely the right time.
Look at the Dragon King’s daughter who was only eight years old.
A divine pearl in his palm radiates precious light;
he has attained the rank of prime minister and court official.
His world-transcending merit and fame cannot be measured by the age.
If one does not even contemplate Amitābha Buddha by his very nature,
I do not know how one can hope to resist impermanence.
Every master of equal standing constantly exhorts people [to do so].
If one does not diligently practice the samādhi of one's own mind,
though the body may dwell in a pure white lotus land,
it is all in vain to merely chant the name of Amitābha with the lips.
The universal ground of equality is but mind-only;
noble and base, wise and foolish—none fall into two paths.
Even a lacquer bucket must be taught to break through from bottom to top.
Everyone applies themselves with diligent effort;
when the mechanism moves, the resonance rings forth spontaneously.
Neither Pure Land nor Chan is discussed.
If one thoroughly understands the common characteristics beyond the phrases,
it is like a single string threading together one hundred and eight mani jewels.
